{"_type":"policyAnalysis","title":"Medicaid DSH Allotment Reductions and the Rural Hospital Fiscal Collapse: A State-by-State Impact Analysis for FY2026\u20132028","slug":{"current":"medicaid-dsh-rural-hospital-fiscal-collapse-2026"},"publishedAt":"2026-03-07T09:00:00Z","status":"Active","pillar":"Policy","category":"Regulation & Legislation","impactLevel":"Critical","summary":"Scheduled reductions to Medicaid Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH) allotments under the Affordable Care Act\u2019s statutory sequencing mechanism will eliminate an estimated $8.3 billion in federal payments to safety-net hospitals between FY2026 and FY2028, with rural Critical Access Hospitals bearing a disproportionate share of the burden due to their Medicaid payer mix and structural inability to cross-subsidize losses from commercial volume. This analysis quantifies the per-state fiscal exposure, identifies the 11 states where DSH reductions will push more than 20% of rural hospitals into operating deficits exceeding negative 5% margin, and maps the federal legislative interventions \u2014 including the Rural Hospital Stabilization and DSH Equity Act of 2025 and CMS\u2019s proposed DSH Transition Relief Rule \u2014 that remain the only credible mechanism for avoiding a wave of closures estimated at 47\u201363 facilities by December 2027. CFOs and state Medicaid directors must treat this as an active solvency emergency, not a future budget risk.","body":[{"_key":"blk001","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The Affordable Care Act\u2019s original architects made a calculated bet in 2010: as Medicaid expansion increased coverage rates and reduced uncompensated care burdens, hospitals would need less Disproportionate Share Hospital compensation to remain solvent. Sixteen years later, that bet has proven catastrophically wrong for rural America. Medicaid DSH allotments were supposed to decline as a share of uncompensated care costs fell \u2014 but in states with limited or non-expanded Medicaid programs and persistently high uninsured rates, rural hospitals have continued to absorb uncompensated care volumes that the DSH mechanism was specifically designed to offset. The statutory reduction schedule, paused repeatedly by Congress but never permanently repealed, is now legally active. Beginning in FY2026, cumulative reductions of $8.3 billion over three federal fiscal years are scheduled to flow through state allotment formulas to individual hospitals with no recalibration for rural market conditions, payer mix differentials, or the structural absence of commercial cross-subsidy that urban safety-net hospitals rely upon.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk002","_type":"block","style":"h2","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The DSH Mechanism: How Reductions Flow from Federal Allotment to Hospital Balance Sheet","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk003","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Understanding why DSH reductions hit rural hospitals harder than urban systems requires tracing the payment mechanism from federal appropriation to individual facility. Congress sets a national DSH allotment cap annually; CMS then distributes that cap to states using a formula that weights each state\u2019s Medicaid expenditures and poverty population. States in turn distribute their allotment to qualifying hospitals through state-specific methodologies \u2014 some based on uncompensated care volume, some based on Medicaid inpatient days, and others through hybrid formulas that incorporate both. The critical structural problem for rural hospitals is that most state distribution methodologies were designed for high-volume urban safety-net environments and systematically underweight the per-patient uncompensated care intensity that characterizes low-volume Critical Access Hospitals serving predominantly uninsured and Medicaid populations.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk004","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Under current law, the FY2026 DSH reduction of $2.1 billion represents an 18.4% cut from FY2025 baseline allotments. For a state like Mississippi, which operates 12 Critical Access Hospitals with a combined Medicaid payer mix averaging 44% \u2014 the highest in the nation \u2014 the state-level allotment reduction translates to an estimated $47 million reduction in DSH payments distributed across those facilities. For a hospital generating $22 million in annual net patient revenue, a DSH reduction of $3.8 million does not represent a manageable budget variance. It represents a structural insolvency event that cannot be offset by operational efficiency gains within a single fiscal year. The math is not complicated. The politics of acknowledging it have been.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk005","_type":"block","style":"h3","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The Uncompensated Care Denominator Problem","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk006","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The ACA\u2019s DSH reduction formula assumed that Medicaid expansion would reduce uncompensated care costs proportionally across all hospital types. That assumption held reasonably well for urban academic medical centers with diversified payer mixes, where a 10-percentage-point reduction in uninsured patients meaningfully improved operating margins. It did not hold for rural hospitals in non-expansion states, where the uninsured rate among working-age adults has remained above 18% in counties served by Critical Access Hospitals, compared to a national urban average of 9.2%. CMS\u2019s own actuarial analysis from the 2025 DSH Informational Notice acknowledged this disparity but offered no formula adjustment. File: frontend/sanity/schemaTypes/academyModule.ts

import { defineField, defineType } from 'sanity'

/**
 * academyModule schema
 * Used for HTR Academy course modules — distinct from policyAnalysis articles.
 * Modules have course-specific fields (moduleNumber, courseTitle, learningObjectives,
 * prevModule/nextModule navigation) and share the same blockContent body as articles.
 */
export const academyModuleType = defineType({
  name: 'academyModule',
  title: 'Academy Module',
  type: 'document',

  // Studio preview: show title + module number in the document list
  preview: {
    select: {
      title: 'title',
      moduleNumber: 'moduleNumber',
      courseTitle: 'courseTitle',
    },
    prepare({ title, moduleNumber, courseTitle }) {
      return {
        title: title || 'Untitled Module',
        subtitle: courseTitle
          ? `Module ${moduleNumber ?? '?'} · ${courseTitle}`
          : `Module ${moduleNumber ?? '?'}`,
      }
    },
  },

  fields: [
    // ── Identity ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    defineField({
      name: 'title',
      title: 'Module Title',
      type: 'string',
      validation: (Rule) => Rule.required(),
    }),

    defineField({
      name: 'slug',
      title: 'Slug',
      type: 'slug',
      options: { source: 'title', maxLength: 96 },
      validation: (Rule) => Rule.required(),
    }),

    // ── Course structure ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    defineField({
      name: 'courseTitle',
      title: 'Course Title',
      type: 'string',
      description: 'The parent course this module belongs to (e.g. "Value-Based Care Fundamentals")',
      validation: (Rule) => Rule.required(),
    }),

    defineField({
      name: 'moduleNumber',
      title: 'Module Number',
      type: 'number',
      description: 'Position in the course sequence (1, 2, 3…)',
      validation: (Rule) => Rule.required().integer().positive(),
    }),

    defineField({
      name: 'totalModules',
      title: 'Total Modules in Course',
      type: 'number',
      description: 'Total number of modules in the parent course — used to render progress (e.g. "2 of 5")',
    }),

    // ── Navigation between modules ───────────────────────────────────────────
    defineField({
      name: 'prevModuleSlug',
      title: 'Previous Module Slug',
      type: 'string',
      description: 'Slug of the preceding module (leave blank for Module 1)',
    }),

    defineField({
      name: 'nextModuleSlug',
      title: 'Next Module Slug',
      type: 'string',
      description: 'Slug of the following module (leave blank for final module)',
    }),

    // ── Pillar tag ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    defineField({
      name: 'pillar',
      title: 'Primary Pillar',
      type: 'string',
      description: 'The HTR pillar this module primarily addresses',
      options: {
        list: [
          { title: 'Policy', value: 'Policy' },
          { title: 'Economics', value: 'Economics' },
          { title: 'Technology', value: 'Technology' },
          { title: 'Clinical', value: 'Clinical' },
          { title: 'Equity', value: 'Equity' },
          { title: 'All Pillars', value: 'All' },
        ],
        layout: 'radio',
      },
    }),

    // ── Metadata ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    defineField({
      name: 'level',
      title: 'Level',
      type: 'string',
      options: {
        list: [
          { title: 'Foundational', value: 'Foundational' },
          { title: 'Intermediate', value: 'Intermediate' },
          { title: 'Advanced', value: 'Advanced' },
        ],
        layout: 'radio',
      },
    }),

    defineField({
      name: 'estimatedReadTime',
      title: 'Estimated Read Time (minutes)',
      type: 'number',
      description: 'Approximate time to complete the module',
    }),

    defineField({
      name: 'publishedAt',
      title: 'Published At',
      type: 'datetime',
    }),

    // ── Learning objectives ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    defineField({
      name: 'learningObjectives',
      title: 'Learning Objectives',
      type: 'array',
      of: [{ type: 'string' }],
      description: 'What the learner will be able to do after completing this module (3–5 objectives)',
    }),

    // ── Summary ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    defineField({
      name: 'summary',
      title: 'Summary',
      type: 'text',
      rows: 4,
      description: '3–4 sentence abstract for the module listing page and meta description',
      validation: (Rule) => Rule.required(),
    }),

    // ── Body ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    defineField({
      name: 'body',
      title: 'Body',
      type: 'blockContent',
      description: 'Full module content — same block types as policy analysis articles',
    }),
  ],
})

File: frontend/sanity/schemaTypes/AudioPlayer.tsx
================
interface AudioProps {
  value: {
    title?: string
    url?: string
    summary?: string
  }
}

export default function AudioPlayer({ value }: AudioProps) {
  // If no URL is provided, don't render anything
  if (!value?.url) return null

  return (
    <div className="my-8 rounded-lg border border-gray-200 bg-gray-50 p-6 shadow-sm">
      <div className="mb-4">
        {value.title && <h3 className="text-lg font-bold text-gray-900">{value.title}</h3>}
        {value.summary && <p className="mt-1 text-sm text-gray-600">{value.summary}</p>}
      </div>
      <audio controls className="w-full focus:outline-none">
        <source src={value.url} type="audio/mpeg" />
        Your browser does not support the audio element.
      </audio>
    </div>
  )
}

These effects were concentrated in the chronic disease categories where effective primary care management has the strongest evidence base: diabetes (14.2% reduction in preventable admissions), congestive heart failure (18.7% reduction), and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (12.4% reduction). Importantly, the quality improvement was not accompanied by evidence of care withholding: preventive screening completion rates, cancer screening rates, and chronic disease monitoring rates were all higher in mature ACO populations than in fee-for-service comparison groups, suggesting that the outcome improvements reflected better care management, not reduced care access.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk005","_type":"block","style":"quote","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"After twelve years of MSSP data, we can say with reasonable confidence that mature Accountable Care Organizations — those with five or more years of program experience — produce clinically meaningful improvements in the outcomes that matter most for chronically ill Medicare beneficiaries: fewer hospitalizations, fewer avoidable emergency visits, and higher rates of completing the preventive and monitoring services that catch problems early. Understanding how shared savings actually works — how the benchmark is set, how savings are calculated, and how they are distributed — is the foundation for understanding the economics of most VBC arrangements. The concept is straightforward: CMS calculates how much it would have expected to spend on your attributed patient population if they had remained in traditional fee-for-service Medicare, adjusted for their age, health status, and geographic cost factors. This projected spend is your “benchmark.” If your ACO’s actual spending on that population comes in below the benchmark, the difference is “savings.” You share those savings with CMS according to a pre-agreed formula — typically retaining 40–75% depending on your risk track and quality performance, with CMS keeping the remainder.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk004","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The devil, as always, is in the details. The benchmark calculation uses a three-year historical average of your patient population’s spending, adjusted upward by a national trend factor. For ACOs whose patient populations were already low-cost before joining the program, this creates an immediate structural problem: their benchmark is low, so even excellent care management produces modest absolute savings, making the shared savings payment insufficient to cover the care management infrastructure investment. This is called the “low benchmark problem,” and it is the primary reason that rural and safety-net ACOs, which often already operate lean systems with lower baseline utilization, struggle to generate shared savings large enough to justify Advanced APM participation costs. CMS has modified the benchmark methodology three times since 2012 in response to this problem, most recently in the Pathways to Success Rule of 2018 and the 2023 ACO Primary Care Flex Model, but the fundamental tension between historical benchmarking and equitable VBC participation for already-efficient providers remains unresolved.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk005","_type":"block","style":"h3","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Upside-Only vs. Two-Sided Risk: The Decision That Changes Everything","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk006","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"One of the most consequential decisions a provider organization makes when entering a shared savings arrangement is whether to accept only upside risk — where you share in savings if you beat the benchmark but owe nothing if you miss it — or two-sided risk, where you both share savings and repay losses if spending exceeds the benchmark. This choice has profound implications for the financial planning, working capital requirements, and organizational risk appetite of the participating entity. Upside-only arrangements (MSSP Track 1 and its successors) are appropriate for organizations beginning their VBC journey: they provide financial experience with population cost management without the catastrophic downside scenario of a major loss repayment obligation. Two-sided arrangements (MSSP ENHANCED Track, Direct Contracting, ACO REACH) offer higher shared savings percentages — sometimes up to 80% of savings — but require the organization to maintain actuarial reserves sufficient to cover a loss scenario, typically modeled at 1–3% of benchmark spending.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk007","_type":"code","title":"Shared Savings Contract Economics: MSSP Rather than holding a provider accountable for the total cost of care across an entire attributed population, bundled payments establish a single target price for all the care associated with a specific clinical episode — typically defined as a procedure or hospitalization plus 90 days of post-acute care. If the sum of all actual payments during the episode falls below the target price, the lead provider (typically the hospital or physician group that performed the primary procedure) retains the difference. If actual costs exceed the target, the lead provider repays the excess. The economic logic is straightforward: bundled payments create a direct financial incentive for the hospital performing a hip replacement to care about which skilled nursing facility the patient is discharged to, how long they stay there, and whether they end up readmitted — because all of those costs are included in the bundle.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk011","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"BPCI Advanced, CMS’s current bundled payment program, covers 32 clinical episodes ranging from major joint replacement and cardiac surgery to pneumonia and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease hospitalizations. The program has generated the strongest evidence of any CMS alternative payment model for procedural episodes: a 2024 CMS evaluation found that BPCI Advanced participants reduced episode spending by an average of $2,100 per episode for major joint replacement while maintaining or improving quality outcomes, generating net Medicare savings of $900 million between 2018 and 2023. Critically, these savings came primarily from reductions in post-acute care spending — fewer days in skilled nursing facilities and more patients discharged directly home with home health services — rather than from reductions in the procedural care itself, confirming the bundled payment hypothesis that the primary driver of unnecessary cost in high-volume procedures is the post-acute care tail, not the procedure.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk012","_type":"block","style":"quote","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The bundled payment evidence for joint replacement is about as clean as healthcare economics gets: when you make the hospital financially responsible for what happens after the patient leaves, patients spend less time in nursing homes, have fewer complications, and cost Medicare significantly less money. The same logic applies to any high-volume procedure with a predictable post-acute care pattern. The challenge is applying it to medical conditions where the post-acute trajectory is far less predictable. — Leemore Dafny, Harvard Business School, Health Affairs, 2025.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk013","_type":"block","style":"h2","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Capitation: The Most Advanced — and Most Misunderstood — VBC Model","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk014","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Capitation is the payment model that most completely aligns provider incentives with patient health outcomes, and the one that generates the most anxiety among providers who have not operated under it before. Under capitation, a provider or provider organization receives a fixed payment per enrolled member per month — the “PMPM” rate — and is responsible for delivering or arranging all covered healthcare services for that member, regardless of how much care they actually use. If the member uses more care than the PMPM covers, the provider absorbs the loss. If the member uses less, the provider retains the surplus. This structure creates the strongest possible financial incentive for prevention, care coordination, and early intervention — because every avoided hospitalization translates directly into retained revenue rather than lost fee-for-service income.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk015","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The anxiety around capitation is understandable but often misdirected. The concern most commonly expressed is that capitation incentivizes providers to withhold necessary care — to under-treat rather than over-treat. This concern is real and has historical basis: the managed care capitation models of the 1990s were frequently criticized for exactly this failure, and some HMO capitation arrangements did produce documented under-treatment in specific service categories. But the lesson of the 1990s HMO experience is not that capitation is inherently dangerous. It is that capitation without robust quality measurement, meaningful patient choice, and strong external accountability produces dangerous incentives. Modern capitation models — including Medicare Advantage plans and CMS’s ACO REACH program — include comprehensive quality metric frameworks with financial consequences for poor performance, minimum coverage requirements that prevent service restriction below evidence-based thresholds, and beneficiary rights to seek care outside the network when needed. The capitation model that exists in 2026 is substantively different from the managed care capitation of 1996.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk016","_type":"block","style":"h3","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"How PMPM Rates Are Set: The Actuarial Core of Capitation","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk017","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The financial success or failure of a capitation arrangement is largely determined before any patient is seen, at the point where the PMPM rate is negotiated or set. If the rate is set too low relative to the actual cost of providing care to the enrolled population, no amount of care management efficiency will produce a viable financial model. If the rate is set appropriately — reflecting the health acuity, demographic profile, and social complexity of the enrolled population — a well-managed capitated provider can generate margins of 3–8% while delivering care that is demonstrably better in quality and lower in total cost than the fee-for-service alternative. The actuarial process of setting a PMPM rate involves risk adjustment models that account for enrollee diagnoses, functional status, and social determinants of health, applied to utilization cost data from comparable populations. For Medicare Advantage plans, CMS sets the base rate using the county-level fee-for-service benchmark and adjusts it upward or downward based on each enrollee’s Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) risk score, a diagnosis-based model that attempts to predict expected healthcare utilization for that individual in the coming year.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk018","_type":"block","style":"h2","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The Volume-to-Value Transition: Why the Math Gets Hard Before It Gets Easy","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk019","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The single most common financial mistake health systems make in VBC transitions is underestimating the revenue disruption of the transition period — the window, typically 18 to 36 months, during which care management investments have begun reducing utilization but VBC contract revenue has not yet scaled to replace the lost fee-for-service volume. Consider a regional health system generating $400 million in annual net patient revenue, with 30% of that revenue from inpatient admissions billed on a fee-for-service basis. The system joins MSSP and invests $2 million in care management infrastructure — care coordinators, a risk stratification platform, a post-discharge follow-up program — that begins generating measurable results in year one, reducing its attributed Medicare population’s hospitalization rate by 12%. That 12% reduction represents approximately 240 avoided admissions. At an average net revenue of $8,500 per admission, it also represents a $2.04 million reduction in fee-for-service inpatient revenue. The system’s MSSP shared savings payment for year one, based on total population savings, might be $1.4 million. Net financial impact of year one VBC investment: negative $640,000.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk020","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"This math is not an argument against VBC. It is an argument for understanding VBC as a multi-year financial investment with a specific payback horizon, rather than a year-one revenue enhancement strategy. The financial literature on mature ACO performance consistently shows that organizations reaching their fifth year of MSSP participation generate shared savings payments averaging $312 per attributed beneficiary annually, compared to an average investment cost of $87 per beneficiary in care management infrastructure — a return on investment of approximately 3.6 to 1. The problem is that most health system financial planning cycles operate on one-to-three year horizons, which are too short to capture the full economic benefit of VBC investment. Organizations that have successfully navigated the volume-to-value transition have done so by securing board approval for a five-to-seven year VBC investment thesis with explicit transition period loss projections, rather than attempting to justify each year’s VBC expenditure against that same year’s VBC revenue.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk021","_type":"block","style":"callout","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"For CFOs and Finance Leaders: If your organization is evaluating ACO or Advanced APM participation, your financial model must explicitly project the transition period revenue displacement — the reduction in fee-for-service inpatient and ED revenue that will occur as care management succeeds. An ACO financial model that shows positive net revenue in year one almost certainly has a methodology error, either in the care management cost estimates or in the assumed savings rate. Realistic five-year models typically show a cumulative loss in years one and two, breakeven in year three, and meaningful positive return in years four and five. Present this model honestly to your board, or the VBC investment will be defunded the first time a quarterly loss appears.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk022","_type":"block","style":"h2","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Primary Care Investment as Economic Infrastructure","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk023","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"One of the most powerful and counterintuitive findings in health economics is that investment in primary care produces returns that are comparable to, and in many cases superior to, investment in specialty care infrastructure — not in terms of individual clinical case intensity, but in terms of total population health spending and outcomes. The economic mechanism is straightforward once articulated: primary care reduces the incidence of the expensive downstream events — hospitalizations, emergency visits, specialist procedures, complications of uncontrolled chronic disease — that account for the vast majority of total healthcare spending. You come in for a physical exam: the doctor bills a code for the exam. The doctor orders a blood test: the lab bills a code for each component of the panel. The doctor finds something concerning and refers you to a specialist: the specialist bills for the consultation. You end up in the hospital: the hospital bills for the admission, for each day you stay, for each procedure performed, and for each medication administered. Each service generates a separate claim, each claim generates a separate payment, and the more services that are delivered, the more total revenue the provider earns. There is no mechanism within fee-for-service that rewards a doctor for keeping you healthy enough that you never needed that specialist referral in the first place.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk008","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Fee-for-service was not designed maliciously. It emerged from a logical place in the early history of American medicine, when the primary challenge was access — getting doctors and hospitals built, staffed, and financially sustainable enough to serve a growing industrial population. Paying per service was a simple, auditable, scalable mechanism that worked reasonably well in an era when healthcare was episodic: you got sick, you saw a doctor, you got better, and the transaction was complete. The model’s structural flaws only became catastrophic when the nature of disease in America fundamentally changed. By the 1980s, the leading drivers of healthcare spending were no longer acute infectious diseases or traumatic injuries — they were chronic conditions like diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, conditions that are managed over years and decades rather than treated in a single episode. Fee-for-service has no payment mechanism for management. It has only payment for treatment.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk009","_type":"block","style":"h3","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The Incentive Problem: When Doing More Pays More","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk010","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The central structural failure of fee-for-service is an incentive misalignment between what is financially rewarded and what produces good health outcomes. Consider a patient with Type 2 diabetes. Under fee-for-service, a primary care physician earns a billing code for the office visit in which they counsel the patient about diet, exercise, and medication adherence. That counseling code reimburses at approximately $85 in a typical Medicare fee schedule. If the physician spends an additional 20 minutes with the patient walking through a personalized nutrition plan, creating a written care management protocol, and coordinating with a dietitian, they may bill a care management add-on code worth an additional $40. Total revenue for doing everything right: approximately $125. Now consider what happens if the counseling fails and the patient is admitted to the hospital with a diabetic ketoacidosis crisis. The hospital admission generates approximately $8,400 in Medicare reimbursement. The specialist consultations during the admission add another $1,200. The physician who sees the patient in the hospital earns a hospital visit code. The laboratory earns from daily blood panels. The pharmacy earns from IV insulin. A preventable crisis generates approximately 80 times more revenue than the preventive care that could have avoided it. Fee-for-service does not reward the prevention of that crisis. In a narrow accounting sense, it rewards its occurrence.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk011","_type":"block","style":"callout","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Key Learning Point: Fee-for-service does not reward bad doctors or incentivize harm. Most physicians are deeply committed to their patients’ wellbeing. The problem is structural: the payment system creates financial pressure toward volume and intensity of treatment, even when lower-intensity preventive care would produce better outcomes. Individual clinicians work against this incentive every day — but the aggregate effect of the incentive on system-wide spending and outcomes is measurable and large.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk012","_type":"block","style":"h2","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"What Value-Based Care Actually Means","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk013","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Value-based care (VBC) is a payment philosophy, not a single program or contract type. Its core principle is simple: pay for outcomes, not for activity. Instead of paying a provider for each individual service delivered, value-based payment models reward providers for achieving defined health outcomes for a defined patient population, at a defined cost target. The shift sounds straightforward but has profound implications for how healthcare is organized, staffed, managed, and measured. Under value-based care, a primary care physician managing 500 diabetic patients is financially rewarded if the average HbA1c level across that population improves, if hospital admission rates decline, and if preventive screenings are completed. The physician earns more by keeping patients healthier — which is, intuitively, exactly what we want the payment system to incentivize.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk014","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The term “value” in healthcare has a specific technical definition, first formalized by Harvard Business School professor Michael Porter in his landmark 2006 work on healthcare strategy. Porter defined healthcare value as health outcomes achieved per dollar spent — a deceptively simple ratio with enormous implications. Improving value means either achieving better outcomes at the same cost, achieving the same outcomes at lower cost, or — ideally — achieving better outcomes at lower cost simultaneously. This framing is important because it explicitly rejects the false choice between quality and cost that has dominated American healthcare policy debates for decades. Value-based care does not argue that we should spend less on healthcare. It argues that the spending we do should produce better results, and that a payment system aligned with outcomes will, over time, naturally drive spending toward the interventions that work and away from the interventions that do not.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk015","_type":"block","style":"h3","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The Spectrum of Value-Based Models: Not All VBC Is the Same","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk016","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Value-based care is not a single contract type — it is a spectrum of payment models that differ in how much financial risk is transferred from payers to providers, and how performance is measured and rewarded. Understanding this spectrum is essential because different organizations are at different stages of VBC adoption, and the policy and technology infrastructure required for advanced models is substantially more complex than what beginner models demand. At one end of the spectrum are pay-for-performance models, sometimes called P4P, in which providers continue to receive fee-for-service reimbursement but earn bonus payments — or face modest penalties — based on quality metrics. These models are low-risk for providers and easy to administer but produce only marginal incentive changes because the base fee-for-service revenue structure is unchanged. At the advanced end of the spectrum are full capitation models, in which a provider or provider organization accepts a fixed per-member per-month payment to cover all of a patient population’s healthcare needs, bearing full financial risk for both the cost and quality of care delivered.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk017","_type":"code","title":"The Value-Based Care Payment Model Spectrum: From FFS to Full Capitation","language":"json","code":[{"Model":"Fee-for-Service (Baseline)","Provider Risk Level":"None","Payment Mechanism":"Per service delivered","Quality Accountability":"None","CMS Example Program":"Traditional Medicare","Typical U.S. Adoption":"Still ~40% of payments"},{"Model":"Pay-for-Performance (P4P)","Provider Risk Level":"Low","Payment Mechanism":"FFS + quality bonus/penalty","Quality Accountability":"Process & outcome metrics","CMS Example Program":"Hospital Value-Based Purchasing Program","Typical U.S. Adoption":"~25% of payments"},{"Model":"Bundled Payments","Provider Risk Level":"Medium","Payment Mechanism":"Single payment per episode of care","Quality Accountability":"Outcome quality for defined episode","CMS Example Program":"BPCI Advanced (Bundled Payments for Care Improvement)","Typical U.S. Adoption":"~10% of payments"},{"Model":"Shared Savings (Upside Only)","Provider Risk Level":"Low-Medium","Payment Mechanism":"FFS base + share of savings if cost target met","Quality Accountability":"Population health quality metrics","CMS Example Program":"Medicare Shared Savings Program Track 1","Typical U.S. Adoption":"~12% of payments"},{"Model":"Shared Savings + Risk (Two-Sided)","Provider Risk Level":"Medium-High","Payment Mechanism":"FFS base + savings share; Value-based care is often discussed primarily as a payment reform — an economics issue. But whether VBC actually works in practice, for which patients, in which communities, and under which circumstances, is determined equally by policy design, technology infrastructure, clinical evidence, and equity architecture. The economics of VBC are complex and often counterintuitive. A provider that successfully keeps patients healthy reduces its own revenue under fee-for-service — a phenomenon called the “volume-to-value transition problem.” Managing this transition requires actuarial expertise, working capital reserves, and sophisticated cost accounting capabilities that many rural and safety-net providers do not currently possess. Understanding the financial mechanics of VBC — how shared savings are calculated, what capitation rates cover, and how quality bonuses are structured — is the subject of Module 3.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk023","_type":"block","style":"normal","listItem":"bullet","level":1,"children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The ","marks":[]},{"_type":"span","text":"Technology Pillar","marks":["strong"]},{"_type":"span","text":" asks: Is value-based care operationally possible without advanced data infrastructure? VBC requires providers to measure outcomes across entire patient populations, identify high-risk patients before they deteriorate, coordinate care across multiple settings, and report quality metrics to payers and CMS with precision and timeliness that fee-for-service never demanded. None of this is possible without interoperable electronic health records, health information exchange, and increasingly, artificial intelligence-powered risk stratification tools. The 34% of rural Critical Access Hospitals that lack a fully certified EHR system, and the 41% that are not connected to their state’s health information exchange, face a technology readiness barrier to advanced VBC participation that is as significant as the financial barrier. However, early-stage ACOs show modest or mixed results, and bundled payment programs show strong outcome improvements for high-volume procedures like hip and knee replacement but limited evidence for complex chronic disease management. Several studies have found that providers serving high-proportions of Medicaid, low-income, and rural patients perform worse on standard VBC quality metrics not because they deliver worse care, but because their patient populations face social determinants of health — food insecurity, housing instability, transportation barriers — that are outside clinical control. Understanding its genuine implementation challenges is as important as understanding its theoretical promise, and any course that presents VBC as a straightforward solution to a complex problem is doing learners a disservice. The transition from fee-for-service to value-based payment creates real financial risk for providers during the transition period. A hospital system that begins reducing unnecessary hospitalizations and emergency visits through better care management is simultaneously reducing its own revenue under the portion of its contracts that remain fee-for-service. For a health system operating at a 1–3% operating margin — which describes the majority of rural and community hospitals in the United States — a 5% reduction in inpatient volume while VBC contracts ramp up can create a cash flow crisis that threatens financial stability before the VBC savings materialize. Value-based care requires measuring outcomes — but measuring outcomes in healthcare is genuinely hard. Unlike a manufacturing process where defect rates can be counted precisely, health outcomes are influenced by dozens of variables outside clinical control, including patients’ genetics, behaviors, economic circumstances, housing stability, and social support networks. A diabetic patient who has adequate food, a safe neighborhood for walking, and a job with health insurance is far more likely to achieve target HbA1c levels than an identically diagnosed patient who is food insecure, living in a neighborhood without sidewalks, and uninsured. If a VBC contract measures both providers on the same HbA1c outcome metric without adjusting for these social differences, it is not measuring quality of care — it is measuring the zip code of the patient population. MIPS is designed as a transitional step — it maintains the fee-for-service base payment structure while adding a performance overlay that rewards quality and penalizes inefficiency. {"_type":"policyAnalysis","title":"Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 4: The Technology Pillar — Data, AI, and the Digital Infrastructure That Makes VBC Work","slug":{"current":"vbc-fundamentals-module-4-technology-pillar"},"publishedAt":"2026-03-07T10:00:00Z","status":"Active","pillar":"Technology","category":"Digital Health Infrastructure","impactLevel":"High","summary":"Module 4 of the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course examines the technology infrastructure that value-based care requires to function — and what happens when that infrastructure is missing. This module explains, in plain language, what interoperable electronic health records, health information exchange, and AI-powered risk stratification tools actually do in a VBC context, why 34% of rural Critical Access Hospitals remain technology-unready for advanced VBC participation, and how the federal interoperability agenda — including the 21st Century Cures Act, the CMS Interoperability Rule, and the TEFCA framework — is building the data infrastructure that VBC depends upon. Connecting passengers to flights would be technically possible but operationally chaotic — delays, lost records, missed connections, and dangerous errors would be routine, not exceptional. This is, only slightly exaggerated, the state of health information exchange in the United States as recently as 2019, and in many rural markets as recently as 2024. Value-based care requires something that American healthcare has never had at scale: a reliable, real-time, standards-based system for sharing patient health information across organizational boundaries. Without it, an Accountable Care Organization cannot know that its attributed Medicare patient was admitted to a hospital outside the network last Tuesday. A care coordinator cannot know that a high-risk patient missed their primary care appointment. A risk stratification algorithm cannot identify a patient approaching a high-cost event without complete longitudinal data about their diagnosis history, medication adherence, and recent utilization. Technology is not a nice-to-have for advanced VBC. It is the operating system on which the entire model runs.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk002","_type":"block","style":"h2","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The Three Technology Layers VBC Requires","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk003","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The technology infrastructure that supports effective value-based care can be understood as three interdependent layers, each building on the one below it. The foundation layer is clinical data capture: the electronic health record system that documents every patient encounter, diagnosis, medication, order, and result in a structured, machine-readable format. The second layer is data integration and exchange: the health information exchange infrastructure that connects EHR systems across organizations so that complete patient data is available regardless of where care was delivered. The third layer is analytics and intelligence: the population health management platforms, risk stratification tools, and increasingly AI-powered predictive models that transform raw clinical data into actionable care management intelligence — identifying which patients are at highest risk of imminent high-cost events, which chronic disease patients are overdue for interventions, and which populations are generating the most preventable utilization. Each layer is necessary but not sufficient. Strong EHR implementation without HIE connectivity produces siloed data. HIE connectivity without analytics produces data that no one has the capacity to act on. Analytics without high-quality underlying data produces predictions that are wrong in ways that are hard to detect until they cause harm.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk004","_type":"block","style":"h2","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Electronic Health Records: The Foundation Layer","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk005","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The United States made a massive federal investment in EHR adoption through the HITECH Act of 2009, which appropriated $27 billion in Medicare and Medicaid incentive payments to encourage providers to implement certified EHR systems and demonstrate “meaningful use” — a defined set of capabilities including electronic prescribing, clinical decision support, and patient portal access. By 2021, 88% of hospitals and 78% of office-based physicians had implemented certified EHR systems, a transformation from the 9% hospital adoption rate that existed in 2008. This is one of the most rapid technology adoption curves in the history of any industry, and it created the clinical data foundation that value-based care analytics requires. However, EHR adoption rates mask significant quality variation that is directly relevant to VBC capability. Having a certified EHR does not mean having a fully configured, fully utilized EHR that generates high-quality structured data. Many providers, particularly smaller rural practices and critical access hospitals, implemented EHR systems at the minimum level required to qualify for HITECH incentive payments, resulting in EHR installations that function primarily as billing and documentation tools rather than population health data platforms.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk006","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The VBC-relevant EHR capabilities that matter most are not the basic documentation features that HITECH required, but the advanced data quality and interoperability features that turn an EHR from a digital chart room into a population health intelligence system. This provision was specifically designed to address a well-documented pattern in which EHR vendors and some health systems restricted data sharing with competitors or external partners, creating artificial data silos that served commercial interests at the expense of care coordination. Second, it mandated that all certified EHR systems implement standardized FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) application programming interfaces by 2022, enabling third-party developers to build population health applications that connect directly to EHR data without requiring custom integrations. In a VBC model managing 10,000 attributed patients, a care management team cannot proactively reach out to every patient every month. They need a system that identifies the 300 or 400 patients most likely to have a preventable hospital admission, emergency department visit, or serious clinical deterioration in the next 90 days, so that care coordination resources can be concentrated where they will have the greatest impact. Traditional risk stratification relied on simple actuarial models — patients with the highest total spending in the prior year were assumed to be the highest risk in the coming year. These models are easy to implement but systematically misdirected: they identify patients who were recently sick rather than patients who are about to become sick, missing the early intervention window where care management is most effective and most cost-efficient.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk017","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Modern AI-powered risk stratification uses machine learning models trained on large clinical datasets to predict future utilization risk based on a much richer set of signals than historical spending alone. These models incorporate diagnosis trajectories (the sequence and pattern of diagnoses over time, not just their presence or absence), medication adherence signals derived from pharmacy data and EHR medication reconciliation records, laboratory value trends (a gradually rising HbA1c over three visits is a stronger predictor of near-term hospitalization than a single elevated value), social determinants of health flags derived from screening questionnaires and zip-code-level data, and behavioral health diagnoses and substance use disorder flags that are strongly predictive of high-cost medical utilization. The predictive accuracy of leading AI risk stratification models, as measured by the C-statistic — the probability that the model correctly identifies a patient who will be hospitalized as higher risk than a patient who will not — has improved from approximately 0.70 for traditional claims-based models to 0.82–0.87 for the leading AI models that incorporate multi-modal EHR data, a meaningful improvement that translates directly into better care management targeting and higher ROI on care coordinator time.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk018","_type":"block","style":"h3","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The AI Bias Problem: When Risk Stratification Perpetuates Inequity","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk019","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"AI risk stratification tools carry a well-documented and serious equity risk: because they are trained on historical healthcare utilization data, they tend to encode the biases present in that data. The algorithm learned that low-cost patients were low-need patients, a correlation that held for white patients but produced systematic underestimation of Black patients’ clinical risk. The practical consequence was that Black patients were significantly less likely to be identified for high-intensity care management programs, perpetuating the very care access disparities that VBC is intended to address.   if (v === undefined) {

*** OBJECTIVE ***
Generate a single, high-fidelity, long-form research article as a RAW MINIFIED JSON OBJECT.
This object must strictly adhere to the 'policyAnalysis' Sanity schema.
Think of this as a peer-reviewed journal article combined with an executive intelligence brief —
not a blog post. Depth, specificity, named data, and expert-level argumentation are mandatory.

*** 1. CORE EXECUTION RULES (CRITICAL — DO NOT BREAK THESE) ***
- OUTPUT ONLY THE JSON. No markdown fences (no ```json), no intro sentence, no outro.
- CHARACTER SANITIZATION: Strictly NO raw control characters (\n, \t, \r inside strings).
  Use \u2014 for em dash, \u2019 for right single quote/apostrophe, \u201c/\u201d for curly quotes.
- ESCAPING: All internal double-quotes must be escaped as \". All backslashes as \\.
- MINIFICATION: The entire output must be a single, continuous line of text with no line breaks.

*** 2. REQUIRED FIELD VALUES ***
- "pillar"     : MUST be exactly one of: "Policy" | "Economics" | "Technology" | "Clinical" | "Equity"
- "category"   : MUST match the subcategory label provided in Section 5 (e.g. "Value-Based Care Models")
- "status"     : MUST be exactly one of: "Active" | "Proposed" | "In Committee"
- "impactLevel": MUST be exactly one of: "Critical" | "High" | "Medium"
- "publishedAt": Use the ISO timestamp provided in Section 5. If none given, use current date in format "2026-01-15T09:00:00Z"

*** 3. LENGTH & DEPTH REQUIREMENTS (NON-NEGOTIABLE) ***

MINIMUM BODY BLOCKS: 35 blocks. Target 40-50 blocks for a full-length article.
MINIMUM PROSE WORD COUNT: Each normal paragraph must contain AT LEAST 60 words.
  Do not write short, thin paragraphs. Every paragraph must advance the argument with
  specific data, named programs, dollar figures, named legislation, or expert-level analysis.
  A paragraph that could have been written without domain expertise is not acceptable.

REQUIRED CONTENT STRUCTURE — the article must contain ALL of the following:
  - 1  opening lead paragraph (normal) — sets the crisis, stakes, and scope. No heading before it.
  - 5-7 h2 section headings, each representing a major chapter of the analysis
  - 2-3 h3 sub-headings distributed across sections (never immediately after an h2)
  - 8-12 normal paragraphs of substantive prose — each 60+ words, data-rich
  - 2  quote blocks — high-impact statistics or authoritative assertions with source context
  - 2  callout blocks — one policy implication, one executive action item
  - 2  bullet lists — each with 4-6 items, each item a complete sentence (not a fragment)
  - 1  numbered list — a step-by-step process, ranked findings, or implementation sequence
  - 2  data tables — each with at least 4 rows and 3 columns of real, specific data
  - 1  image block — caption must be a detailed technical description (2-3 sentences)
  - 1  audio block — MANDATORY. Use a plausible HTR podcast URL and write a substantive summary.
  - 1  video block — MANDATORY. Use a plausible YouTube URL and write a substantive caption.

DEPTH STANDARDS — every article must include:
  - At least 6 specific dollar figures, percentages, or quantitative data points
  - At least 3 named federal programs, legislation, or regulatory rules (e.g. CONNECT Act, CMS AHEAD Model)
  - At least 2 named geographic examples (states, regions, or specific health systems)
  - At least 1 forward-looking projection or scenario analysis
  - A conclusion section (h2: "Executive Takeaway" or similar) with concrete next steps

*** 4. BODY COMPONENT RULES (THE "NEVER-FAIL" RULES) ***

CRITICAL: Every item in the "body" array MUST have a unique "_key" field.
Format: "_key": "blk[sequential_3digit_number]"  e.g. "blk001", "blk002", "blk003" ... "blk042"

HEADING HIERARCHY RULES (enforce strictly):
- Use h2 for MAJOR section breaks (5-7 per article). Think of these as chapter titles.
- Use h3 for sub-points WITHIN a section. An h3 must always appear after an h2, never before.
- NEVER place two h2 blocks back-to-back without at least two normal paragraphs between them.
- NEVER place an h3 immediately after an h2 — always write at least one normal paragraph first.
- The article must NOT open with a heading. The first block must always be a normal paragraph.
- Natural rhythm: h2 -> paragraph -> paragraph -> h3 -> paragraph -> paragraph -> quote -> h2...

*** OBJECTIVE ***
Generate a single, high-fidelity research article as a RAW MINIFIED JSON OBJECT.
This object must strictly adhere to the 'policyAnalysis' Sanity schema.

*** 1. CORE EXECUTION RULES (CRITICAL — DO NOT BREAK THESE) ***
- OUTPUT ONLY THE JSON. No markdown fences (no ```json), no intro sentence, no outro.
- CHARACTER SANITIZATION: Strictly NO raw control characters (\n, \t, \r inside strings).
  Use \u2014 for em dash, \u2019 for right single quote/apostrophe, \u201c/\u201d for curly quotes.
- ESCAPING: All internal double-quotes must be escaped as \". All backslashes as \\.
- MINIFICATION: The entire output must be a single, continuous line of text with no line breaks.

*** 2. REQUIRED FIELD VALUES ***
- "pillar"     : MUST be exactly one of: "Policy" | "Economics" | "Technology" | "Clinical" | "Equity"
- "category"   : MUST match the subcategory label provided in Section 4 (e.g. "Value-Based Care Models")
- "status"     : MUST be exactly one of: "Active" | "Proposed" | "In Committee"
- "impactLevel": MUST be exactly one of: "Critical" | "High" | "Medium"
- "publishedAt": Use the ISO timestamp provided in Section 4. If none given, use current date in format "2026-01-15T09:00:00Z"

*** 3. BODY COMPONENT RULES (THE "NEVER-FAIL" RULES) ***

CRITICAL: Every item in the "body" array MUST have a unique "_key" field.
Format: "_key": "blk[sequential_3digit_number]"  e.g. "blk001", "blk002", "blk003"...

MINIMUM BODY REQUIREMENT: Generate AT LEAST 12 body blocks. A research article should include:
- 1 lead paragraph (normal) — no heading before it; drop the reader directly into the argument
- 2–4 h2 section headings, each followed by 2–3 normal paragraphs before the next h2
- 1–2 h3 sub-headings used WITHIN a section to break a complex argument into named parts
- 1 quote block (a key statistic or expert-level assertion)
- 1 callout block (a policy implication, alert, or action item)
- 1 data table (code block with language json)
- 1 image block (caption + alt only — NO asset or _ref field)
- Optional: 1 audio or video block if a briefing URL is provided

HEADING HIERARCHY RULES (enforce strictly):
- Use h2 for MAJOR section breaks only (2–4 per article). Think of these as chapter titles.
- Use h3 for sub-points WITHIN a section. An h3 must always appear after an h2, never before.
- NEVER place two h2 blocks back-to-back without at least one normal paragraph between them.
- NEVER place an h3 immediately after an h2 — always write at least one normal paragraph first.
- The article must NOT open with a heading. The first block must always be a normal paragraph.
- Aim for a natural reading rhythm: h2 → paragraph → paragraph → h3 → paragraph → quote/callout → h2...

const fs = require("fs");
const path = require("path");
const { createClient } = require("@sanity/client");

// --- 1. CONFIGURATION LOADING ---
function loadEnv() {
  const paths = [
    path.resolve(__dirname, ".env.local"),
    path.resolve(__dirname, "../.env.local"),
    path.resolve(__dirname, "../../.env.local"),
  ];

  for (const p of paths) {
    if (fs.existsSync(p)) {
      const content = fs.readFileSync(p, "utf8");
      content.split("\n").forEach((line) => {
        const [key, ...values] = line.split("=");
        if (key && values.length > 0) {
          const val = values.join("=").trim().replace(/^["']|["']$/g, "");
          process.env[key.trim()] = val;
        }
      });
      return;
    }
  }
}

loadEnv();

if (!process.env.SANITY_API_TOKEN) {
  console.error("❌ Error: SANITY_API_TOKEN is missing in .env.local.");
  process.exit(1);
}

const client = createClient({
  projectId: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID,
  dataset: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET || "production",
  token: process.env.SANITY_API_TOKEN,
  apiVersion: "2026-02-19",
  useCdn: false,
});

// Adjusted to look for /sanity/content relative to the script location
const CONTENT_DIR = path.join(__dirname, "../sanity/content");

function generateKey() {
  return Math.random().toString(36).substring(2, 10);
}

// --- 2. HELPER: Data Sanitization (Maintained from your original) ---
function sanitizeBlock(block) {
  if (!block._key) block._key = generateKey();

  if (block._type === "code") {
    if (Array.isArray(block.code)) {
      block.code = JSON.stringify(block.code, null, 2);
    }
    if (!block.language) block.language = "json";
  }

  if (block._type === "video" && block.url && block.url.startsWith("[")) {
    const match = block.url.match(/\((https?:\/\/[^)]+)\)/);
    if (match && match[1]) block.url = match[1];
  }

  if (block.children && Array.isArray(block.children)) {
    block.children = block.children.map((child) => {
      if (!child._key) child._key = generateKey();
      return child;
    });
  }
  return block;
}

// --- 3. BULK EXECUTION LOGIC ---
async function bulkImport() {
  if (!fs.existsSync(CONTENT_DIR)) {
    console.error(`❌ Error: Content directory not found at ${CONTENT_DIR}`);
    process.exit(1);
  }

  const files = fs.readdirSync(CONTENT_DIR).filter(file => file.endsWith(".json"));
  
  if (files.length === 0) {
    console.log("⚠️ No JSON files found in sanity/content.");
    return;
  }

  console.log(`🚀 Found ${files.length} files. Starting bulk upload...`);

  for (const file of files) {
    const fullPath = path.join(CONTENT_DIR, file);
    
    try {
      const rawData = fs.readFileSync(fullPath, "utf8");
      const firstBrace = rawData.indexOf("{");
      const lastBrace = rawData.lastIndexOf("}");
      
      if (firstBrace === -1 || lastBrace === -1) {
        console.warn(`⏩ Skipping ${file}: No valid JSON object found.`);
        continue;
      }

      const doc = JSON.parse(rawData.substring(firstBrace, lastBrace + 1));

      // Use slug as _id to ensure 'createOrReplace' performs an overwrite
      const documentId = doc.slug?.current || file.replace(".json", "");

      if (doc.body && Array.isArray(doc.body)) {
        doc.body = doc.body.map(sanitizeBlock);
      }

      await client.createOrReplace({
        _id: documentId,
        _type: "policyAnalysis",
        ...doc,
      });

      console.log(`✅ Imported/Updated: "${doc.title}" (${file})`);
    } catch (err) {
      console.error(`❌ Failed ${file}: ${err.message}`);
    }
  }

  console.log("\n✨ Bulk import process complete.");
}

bulkImport();

// scripts/import_course.js
// Auto-creates a `course` document in Sanity for each unique courseTitle
// found among your imported academyModule documents.
//
// Usage: node scripts/import_course.js
// No arguments needed — it reads directly from Sanity.

const { createClient } = require("@sanity/client");
const path = require("path");

require("dotenv").config({ path: path.resolve(__dirname, "../.env.local") });

const { SANITY_API_TOKEN, NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID, NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET } = process.env;

if (!SANITY_API_TOKEN) {
  console.error("❌ SANITY_API_TOKEN is missing from .env.local");
  process.exit(1);
}
if (!NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID) {
  console.error("❌ NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID is missing from .env.local");
  process.exit(1);
}

const client = createClient({
  projectId: NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID,
  dataset: NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET || "production",
  token: SANITY_API_TOKEN,
  apiVersion: "2024-01-01",
  useCdn: false,
});

// Valid pillar values for the `course` schema
const COURSE_PILLARS = ["Policy", "Economics", "Technology", "Operations"];

function slugify(text) {
  return text
    .toLowerCase()
    .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-")
    .replace(/^-|-$/g, "");
}

async function run() {
  // Fetch all imported academy modules
  const modules = await client.fetch(
    `*[_type == "academyModule"] | order(moduleNumber asc) {
      _id,
      title,
      courseTitle,
      moduleNumber,
      pillar,
      level,
      summary
    }`
  );

  if (modules.length === 0) {
    console.error("❌ No academyModule documents found in Sanity. Import modules first.");
    process.exit(1);
  }

  // Group modules by courseTitle
  const grouped = modules.reduce((acc, mod) => {
    const key = mod.courseTitle;
    if (!acc[key]) acc[key] = [];
    acc[key].push(mod);
    return acc;
  }, {});

  console.log(`Found ${Object.keys(grouped).length} course(s) across ${modules.length} modules:\n`);

  for (const [courseTitle, mods] of Object.entries(grouped)) {
    const slug = slugify(courseTitle);
    const docId = `course-${slug}`;

    // Use the first module's pillar if it's valid for courses, otherwise leave unset
    const rawPillar = mods[0]?.pillar;
    const pillar = COURSE_PILLARS.includes(rawPillar) ? rawPillar : undefined;

    const doc = {
      _id: docId,
      _type: "course",
      title: courseTitle,
      slug: { _type: "slug", current: slug },
      description: mods[0]?.summary ?? "",
      type: "COURSE",
      meta: `${mods.length} Module${mods.length !== 1 ? "s" : ""} • Self-Paced`,
      ...(pillar && { pillar }),
      // Reference each module in order; _key required on all array items in Sanity
      modules: mods.map((m) => ({
        _type: "reference",
        _ref: m._id,
        _key: Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10),
      })),
    };

    await client.createOrReplace(doc);

    console.log(`✅ "${courseTitle}"`);
    console.log(`   ID    : ${docId}`);
    console.log(`   Slug  : /academy/courses/${slug}`);
    console.log(`   Modules: ${mods.map((m) => `#${m.moduleNumber}`).join(", ")}\n`);
  }

  console.log("Done. Open /academy?tab=courses to see your courses.");
}

run().catch((err) => {
  console.error("❌ Error:", err.message);
  process.exit(1);
});

#!/usr/bin/env npx tsx
/**
 * scripts/seed-sanity-performance-index.ts
 *
 * Seeds statePerformanceIndex documents in Sanity from the static
 * performance-index-data.ts file.
 * Run once to migrate; after that, edit scores in the Sanity Studio.
 *
 * Usage:
 *   npx tsx scripts/seed-sanity-performance-index.ts
 *
 * Prerequisites:
 *   - SANITY_API_TOKEN (write token) must be in .env.local or shell env.
 *   - NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID and NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET must be set.
 *   - Run this AFTER deploying the statePerformanceIndex schema to Sanity Studio.
 */

import * as dotenv from "dotenv";
import path from "path";
dotenv.config({ path: path.resolve(__dirname, "../.env.local") });

import { createClient } from "@sanity/client";
import { performanceIndexData } from "../lib/data/performance-index-data";

const sanity = createClient({
  projectId: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID!,
  dataset: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET || "production",
  apiVersion: "2024-01-01",
  token: process.env.SANITY_API_TOKEN,
  useCdn: false,
});

async function main() {
  const states = Object.values(performanceIndexData);
  console.log(`Seeding ${states.length} statePerformanceIndex documents…`);

  for (const state of states) {
    const docId = `perfIndex-${state.id}`;
    const doc = {
      _id: docId,
      _type: "statePerformanceIndex",
      stateId: { _type: "slug", current: state.id },
      stateName: state.stateName,
      performanceScore: state.performanceScore,
      status: state.status,
      policyMetrics: {
        vbpAdoption: state.metrics.policy.vbpAdoption,
        telehealth: state.metrics.policy.telehealth,
        scopeOfPractice: state.metrics.policy.scopeOfPractice,
      },
      economicsMetrics: {
        spendingPerCapita: state.metrics.economics.spendingPerCapita,
        workforceGaps: state.metrics.economics.workforceGaps,
        insuranceCoverage: state.metrics.economics.insuranceCoverage,
      },
      technologyMetrics: {
        hieAdoption: state.metrics.technology.hieAdoption,
        broadbandAccess: state.metrics.technology.broadbandAccess,

#!/usr/bin/env npx tsx
/**
 * scripts/seed-sanity-rht.ts
 *
 * Seeds rhtState documents in Sanity from the static rht-program.ts data.
 * Run once to migrate; after that, edit RHT state profiles in the Sanity Studio.
 *
 * Usage:
 *   npx tsx scripts/seed-sanity-rht.ts
 *
 * Prerequisites:
 *   - SANITY_API_TOKEN (write token) must be in .env.local or shell env.
 *   - NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID and NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET must be set.
 *   - Run this AFTER deploying the rhtState schema to Sanity Studio.
 */

import * as dotenv from "dotenv";
import path from "path";
dotenv.config({ path: path.resolve(__dirname, "../.env.local") });

import { createClient } from "@sanity/client";
import { rhtProgramData } from "../lib/data/rht-program";

const sanity = createClient({
  projectId: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID!,
  dataset: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET || "production",
  apiVersion: "2024-01-01",
  token: process.env.SANITY_API_TOKEN,
  useCdn: false,
});

async function main() {
  const states = Object.values(rhtProgramData);
  console.log(`Seeding ${states.length} rhtState documents…`);

  for (const state of states) {
    const docId = `rhtState-${state.id}`;
    const doc = {
      _id: docId,
      _type: "rhtState",
      stateId: { _type: "slug", current: state.id },
      stateName: state.stateName,
      awardAmount: state.awardAmount,
      status: state.status ?? "Active",
      strategicFocus: Array.isArray(state.strategicFocus)
        ? state.strategicFocus.join(", ")
        : state.strategicFocus,
      description: state.description,
      initiatives: (state.initiatives ?? []).map((ini, i) => ({
        _key: `ini-${i}`,
        title: ini.title,
        description: ini.description,
      })),
      metrics: (state.metrics ?? []).map((m, i) => ({
        _key: `metric-${i}`,
        label: m.label,
        status: m.status,
        target: m.target ?? "",
      })),
    };

    await sanity.createOrReplace(doc);
    console.log(`  ✓ ${state.stateName}`);
  }

  console.log("\nDone. All rhtState documents seeded.");
}

main().catch((err) => {
  console.error(err);
  process.exit(1);
});

const { createClient } = require("@supabase/supabase-js");
const { createClient: createSanityClient } = require("next-sanity");
const path = require("path");
const fs = require("fs");

// 1. Load Environment Variables
function loadEnv() {
  const paths = [path.resolve(__dirname, ".env.local"), path.resolve(__dirname, "../.env.local")];
  for (const p of paths) {
    if (fs.existsSync(p)) {
      const content = fs.readFileSync(p, "utf8");
      content.split("\n").forEach((line) => {
        const [key, ...values] = line.split("=");
        if (key) process.env[key.trim()] = values.join("=").trim().replace(/^["']|["']$/g, "");
      });
      return;
    }
  }
}
loadEnv();

// 2. Initialize Clients
const sanity = createSanityClient({
  projectId: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID,
  dataset: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET || "production",
  token: process.env.SANITY_API_TOKEN,
  apiVersion: "2023-10-01",
  useCdn: false,
});

// USE THE SERVICE ROLE KEY (Bypasses RLS)
const supabaseAdmin = createClient(
  process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL,
  process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY
);

async function seedSupabase() {
  console.log("🔌 Connecting with Admin Privileges...");

  // A. FETCH SANITY CONTENT
  const courses = await sanity.fetch(`*[_type == "course"]{_id, title}`);
  const reports = await sanity.fetch(`*[_type == "report"]{_id, title}`);

  if (courses.length === 0) throw new Error("No courses found in Sanity. Run seed-courses.js first.");

  // B. GET OR CREATE USER (Using Admin API)
  const email = "aris.thorne@htr.com";
  
  console.log(`👤 Checking for user: ${email}...`);
  
  // 1. Check if user exists using Admin API
  const { data: { users }, error: listError } = await supabaseAdmin.auth.admin.listUsers();
  if (listError) throw new Error(`List Users Failed: ${listError.message}`);

  let user = users.find(u => u.email === email);
  let userId;

  if (user) {
    console.log("   User already exists.");
    userId = user.id;
  } else {
    console.log("   Creating new user...");
    const { data: newUser, error: createError } = await supabaseAdmin.auth.admin.createUser({
      email,
      password: "password123",
      email_confirm: true, // Auto-confirm email
      user_metadata: {
        full_name: "Dr. Aris Thorne",
        avatar_url: ""
      }
    });
    
    if (createError) throw new Error(`Create User Failed: ${createError.message}`);
    userId = newUser.user.id;
  }

  console.log(`✅ Target User ID: ${userId}`);

  // C. SEED ENROLLMENTS (Using Admin Client to Bypass RLS)
  const enrollments = courses.slice(0, 2).map(c => ({
    user_id: userId,
    sanity_course_id: c._id,
    progress: Math.floor(Math.random() * 60) + 10
  }));

  const { error: enrollError } = await supabaseAdmin
    .from('enrollments')
    .upsert(enrollments, { onConflict: 'user_id, sanity_course_id' });

  if (enrollError) {
    console.error("❌ Enrollment Error:", enrollError);
  } else {
    console.log(`✅ Successfully linked ${enrollments.length} courses to user.`);
  }

  // D. SEED SAVED REPORTS
  if (reports.length > 0) {
    const savedReports = [{
      user_id: userId,
      sanity_report_id: reports[0]._id
    }];

    const { error: reportError } = await supabaseAdmin
      .from('saved_reports')
      .upsert(savedReports, { onConflict: 'user_id, sanity_report_id' });
      
    if (reportError) console.error("❌ Report Error:", reportError);
    else console.log(`✅ Successfully linked 1 report to user.`);
  }

  console.log("🚀 Seeding Complete.");
}

seedSupabase().catch(err => console.error(err));

File: frontend/bulk_import.js

const fs = require('fs');
const path = require('path');
const { createClient } = require('@sanity/client');

// Initialize the client
const client = createClient({
  projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
  dataset: 'production',
  useCdn: false,
  token: 'YOUR_WRITE_TOKEN', // You need a token with write access from manage.sanity.io
  apiVersion: '2026-03-02',
});

const contentDir = path.join(__dirname, 'sanity/content');

async function bulkImport() {
  const files = fs.readdirSync(contentDir).filter(file => file.endsWith('.json'));
  
  console.log(`Found ${files.length} files. Starting bulk upload...`);

  for (const file of files) {
    try {
      const filePath = path.join(contentDir, file);
      const rawData = fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf-8');
      const doc = JSON.parse(rawData);

      // Ensure the document has an _id based on the filename if one isn't present
      // This ensures that re-running the script "overwrites" instead of duplicating.
      if (!doc._id) {
        doc._id = file.replace('.json', '').replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9]/g, '-');
      }

      console.log(`Uploading: ${doc.title || file}...`);
      
      // .createOrReplace() is exactly what you asked for: 
      // It loads new ones and overwrites existing ones.
      await client.createOrReplace(doc);
      
    } catch (err) {
      console.error(`Error processing ${file}:`, err.message);
    }
  }
  console.log('Bulk import complete.');
}

bulkImport();

import os
import re

def read_file(path):
    print(f"\n--- START FILE: {path} ---")
    try:
        with open(path, 'r', encoding='utf-8', errors='ignore') as f:
            print(f.read())
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"[Error reading: {e}]")
    print(f"--- END FILE: {path} ---")

def run():
    content_dir = "frontend/sanity/content"
    
    # 1. Find the latest article files
    if os.path.exists(content_dir):
        files = os.listdir(content_dir)
        # Filter for article-like json files
        article_files = [f for f in files if f.endswith('.json') and 'article' in f.lower()]
        
        # Sort them to find the latest (simple alphanumeric sort)
        article_files.sort()
        
        # Pick the last 3 files (likely the most recent versions)
        targets = article_files[-3:] if len(article_files) > 3 else article_files
        
        print(f"Found latest articles: {targets}")
        
        for f in targets:
            read_file(os.path.join(content_dir, f))
    else:
        print(f"Directory not found: {content_dir}")

    # 2. Check for the Prompt Template
    prompt_path = "frontend/sanity/prompt_template_draft.txt"
    if os.path.exists(prompt_path):
        read_file(prompt_path)
    else:
        print(f"\n[!] Prompt draft not found at: {prompt_path}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

            A weighted calculation engine quantifying health system maturity across Clinical, Economic, and Social domains.
          </p>
        </div>

          {['hospital', 'region', 'state'].map(lvl => (
            <button
              key={lvl}
              onClick={() => setLevel(lvl)}
              className={`px-6 py-2.5 rounded-xl text-xs font-bold uppercase tracking-widest transition-all ${
                level === lvl ? 'bg-white text-indigo-600 shadow-xl border border-slate-100' : 'text-slate-400 hover:text-slate-600'
              }`}
            >
              {lvl}
            </button>
          ))}
        </div>
      </div>

      <div className="grid grid-cols-1 lg:grid-cols-12 gap-10">
        
        {/* Metric Modifiers */}
        <div className="lg:col-span-4 space-y-8">
          <div className="bg-slate-900 rounded-[2rem] p-10 text-white shadow-2xl relative overflow-hidden group">
            <div className="relative z-10">
              <p className="text-indigo-400 font-black text-xs uppercase tracking-[0.2em] mb-4">Composite Score</p>
              <div className="flex items-baseline gap-3 mb-4">
                <span className="text-8xl font-black tracking-tighter">{compositeScore}</span>
                <span className="text-slate-400 font-bold text-xl italic">/ 100</span>
              </div>
              <div className="flex items-center gap-2">
                <div className={`w-3 h-3 rounded-full ${parseFloat(compositeScore) > 70 ? 'bg-emerald-400' : 'bg-orange-400'} animate-pulse`}></div>
                <span className="text-sm font-bold text-slate-300 tracking-wide">Maturity: {parseFloat(compositeScore) > 70 ? 'Advanced' : 'Intervention Needed'}</span>

              <Zap size={14} className="text-indigo-600" />
            </h3>
            <div className="space-y-8">
              {HTI_WEIGHTS.map(m => (
                <div key={m.id} className="group">
                  <div className="flex justify-between text-[10px] font-bold mb-3 uppercase tracking-wider">

                    <span className="text-slate-900 bg-slate-50 px-2 py-0.5 rounded">{metrics[m.id as keyof typeof metrics]}%</span>
                  </div>
                  <input 
                    type="range" 
                    min="0" max="100" 
                    value={metrics[m.id as keyof typeof metrics]}
                    onChange={(e) => setMetrics(prev => ({ ...prev, [m.id]: parseInt(e.target.value) }))}
                    className="w-full h-1.5 bg-slate-100 rounded-full appearance-none cursor-pointer accent-indigo-600"
                  />
                </div>
              ))}
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>

        {/* Maturity Visualization */}
        <div className="lg:col-span-8 space-y-10">
          <div className="bg-white rounded-[2rem] shadow-xl border border-slate-100 p-10 flex flex-col items-center min-h-[550px]">
             <div className="w-full flex justify-between items-center mb-10">
               <h3 className="font-black text-slate-900 text-lg uppercase tracking-tight">Maturity Radar Chart</h3>
               <button className="text-xs font-bold text-indigo-600 border border-indigo-100 px-4 py-2 rounded-xl hover:bg-indigo-50 transition-all flex items-center gap-2">
                 <ArrowUpRight size={14} /> Export Dataset
               </button>
             </div>
             <div className="w-full max-w-xl h-[450px]">
               <Radar 
                data={radarData} 
                options={{
                  maintainAspectRatio: false,
