{"_type":"academyModule","title":"Value-Based Care Fundamentals \u2014 Module 3: The Economics Pillar \u2014 Following the Money in Value-Based Care","slug":{"current":"vbc-fundamentals-module-3-economics-pillar"},"publishedAt":"2026-03-07T10:00:00Z","pillar":"Economics","summary":"Module 3 of the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course examines the financial mechanics of value-based care from first principles. It explains, in plain language, how money actually flows in the major VBC contract structures \u2014 shared savings, bundled payments, and capitation \u2014 how providers calculate whether a VBC arrangement is financially rational for their organization, what the volume-to-value transition problem means in practice for health system balance sheets, and what the economic evidence says about which VBC models generate durable savings versus which ones simply shift cost without reducing it. Learners will leave this module able to evaluate a VBC contract term sheet, identify the key actuarial concepts their finance teams are using, and understand the economic case for primary care investment as the highest-return infrastructure spend in healthcare.","body":[{"_key":"blk001","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Here is a question that sounds simple but is genuinely hard to answer: if a hospital successfully reduces its patients\u2019 hospitalization rate by 15% through better care management, is that good news or bad news for the hospital\u2019s finances? The instinctive answer is that it must be good news \u2014 fewer hospitalizations means healthier patients, which is surely the goal. But in a world where 40% of that hospital\u2019s revenue still comes from fee-for-service Medicare and Medicaid payments, fewer hospitalizations means fewer inpatient admissions, which means fewer billed days, which means lower revenue. The hospital just cut its own income by doing its job better. This is not a hypothetical paradox \u2014 it is the central economic tension of the volume-to-value transition, experienced by virtually every health system that has seriously engaged with value-based care. Understanding this tension, and the financial mechanisms that VBC contract structures use to resolve it, is what this module is about.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk002","_type":"block","style":"h2","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The Financial Anatomy of a Shared Savings Contract","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk003","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The Medicare Shared Savings Program is the most widely adopted VBC model in the United States, and shared savings is the financial mechanism at its core. Understanding how shared savings actually works \u2014 how the benchmark is set, how savings are calculated, and how they are distributed \u2014 is the foundation for understanding the economics of most VBC arrangements. The concept is straightforward: CMS calculates how much it would have expected to spend on your attributed patient population if they had remained in traditional fee-for-service Medicare, adjusted for their age, health status, and geographic cost factors. This projected spend is your \u201cbenchmark.\u201d If your ACO\u2019s actual spending on that population comes in below the benchmark, the difference is \u201csavings.\u201d You share those savings with CMS according to a pre-agreed formula \u2014 typically retaining 40\u201375% depending on your risk track and quality performance, with CMS keeping the remainder.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk004","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The devil, as always, is in the details. The benchmark calculation uses a three-year historical average of your patient population\u2019s spending, adjusted upward by a national trend factor. For ACOs whose patient populations were already low-cost before joining the program, this creates an immediate structural problem: their benchmark is low, so even excellent care management produces modest absolute savings, making the shared savings payment insufficient to cover the care management infrastructure investment. This is called the \u201clow benchmark problem,\u201d and it is the primary reason that rural and safety-net ACOs, which often already operate lean systems with lower baseline utilization, struggle to generate shared savings large enough to justify Advanced APM participation costs. CMS has modified the benchmark methodology three times since 2012 in response to this problem, most recently in the Pathways to Success Rule of 2018 and the 2023 ACO Primary Care Flex Model, but the fundamental tension between historical benchmarking and equitable VBC participation for already-efficient providers remains unresolved.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk005","_type":"block","style":"h3","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Upside-Only vs. Two-Sided Risk: The Decision That Changes Everything","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk006","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"One of the most consequential decisions a provider organization makes when entering a shared savings arrangement is whether to accept only upside risk \u2014 where you share in savings if you beat the benchmark but owe nothing if you miss it \u2014 or two-sided risk, where you both share savings and repay losses if spending exceeds the benchmark. This choice has profound implications for the financial planning, working capital requirements, and organizational risk appetite of the participating entity. Upside-only arrangements (MSSP Track 1 and its successors) are appropriate for organizations beginning their VBC journey: they provide financial experience with population cost management without the catastrophic downside scenario of a major loss repayment obligation. Two-sided arrangements (MSSP ENHANCED Track, Direct Contracting, ACO REACH) offer higher shared savings percentages \u2014 sometimes up to 80% of savings \u2014 but require the organization to maintain actuarial reserves sufficient to cover a loss scenario, typically modeled at 1\u20133% of benchmark spending.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk007","_type":"code","title":"Shared Savings Contract (Two-Sided)":"$1.6-$2.0M","ACO REACH (Full Risk)":"$2.5M"}]},{"_key":"blk008","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The financial model in the table above illustrates why Two-Sided and Full-Risk tracks are substantially more attractive in their best-case financial outcome \u2014 but also why the actuarial reserve requirement creates a genuine barrier to entry for Rather than holding a provider accountable for the total cost of care across an entire attributed population, bundled payments establish a single target price for all the care associated with a specific clinical episode \u2014 typically defined as a procedure or hospitalization plus 90 days of post-acute care. If the sum of all actual payments during the episode falls below the target price, the lead provider (typically the hospital or physician group that performed the primary procedure) retains the difference. If actual costs exceed the target, the lead provider repays the excess. The economic logic is straightforward: bundled payments create a direct financial incentive for the hospital performing a hip replacement to care about which skilled nursing facility the patient is discharged to, how long they stay there, and whether they end up readmitted \u2014 because all of those costs are included in the bundle.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk011","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"BPCI Advanced, CMS\u2019s current bundled payment program, covers 32 clinical episodes ranging from major joint replacement and cardiac surgery to pneumonia and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease hospitalizations. The program has generated the strongest evidence of any CMS alternative payment model for procedural episodes: a 2024 CMS evaluation found that BPCI Advanced participants reduced episode spending by an average of $2,100 per episode for major joint replacement while maintaining or improving quality outcomes, generating net Medicare savings of $900 million between 2018 and 2023. Critically, these savings came primarily from reductions in post-acute care spending \u2014 fewer days in skilled nursing facilities and more patients discharged directly home with home health services \u2014 rather than from reductions in the procedural care itself, confirming the bundled payment hypothesis that the primary driver of unnecessary cost in high-volume procedures is the post-acute care tail, not the procedure.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk012","_type":"block","style":"quote","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The bundled payment evidence for joint replacement is about as clean as healthcare economics gets: when you make the hospital financially responsible for what happens after the patient leaves, patients spend less time in nursing homes, have fewer complications, and cost Medicare significantly less money. The same logic applies to any high-volume procedure with a predictable post-acute care pattern. The challenge is applying it to medical conditions where the post-acute trajectory is far less predictable. \u2014 Leemore Dafny, Harvard Business School, Health Affairs, 2025.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk013","_type":"block","style":"h2","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Capitation: The Most Advanced \u2014 and Most Misunderstood \u2014 VBC Model","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk014","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Capitation is the payment model that most completely aligns provider incentives with patient health outcomes, and the one that generates the most anxiety among providers who have not operated under it before. Under capitation, a provider or provider organization receives a fixed payment per enrolled member per month \u2014 the \u201cPMPM\u201d rate \u2014 and is responsible for delivering or arranging all covered healthcare services for that member, regardless of how much care they actually use. If the member uses more care than the PMPM covers, the provider absorbs the loss. If the member uses less, the provider retains the surplus. This structure creates the strongest possible financial incentive for prevention, care coordination, and early intervention \u2014 because every avoided hospitalization translates directly into retained revenue rather than lost fee-for-service income.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk015","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The anxiety around capitation is understandable but often misdirected. The concern most commonly expressed is that capitation incentivizes providers to withhold necessary care \u2014 to under-treat rather than over-treat. This concern is real and has historical basis: the managed care capitation models of the 1990s were frequently criticized for exactly this failure, and some HMO capitation arrangements did produce documented under-treatment in specific service categories. But the lesson of the 1990s HMO experience is not that capitation is inherently dangerous. It is that capitation without robust quality measurement, meaningful patient choice, and strong external accountability produces dangerous incentives. Modern capitation models \u2014 including Medicare Advantage plans and CMS\u2019s ACO REACH program \u2014 include comprehensive quality metric frameworks with financial consequences for poor performance, minimum coverage requirements that prevent service restriction below evidence-based thresholds, and beneficiary rights to seek care outside the network when needed. The capitation model that exists in 2026 is substantively different from the managed care capitation of 1996.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk016","_type":"block","style":"h3","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"How PMPM Rates Are Set: The Actuarial Core of Capitation","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk017","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The financial success or failure of a capitation arrangement is largely determined before any patient is seen, at the point where the PMPM rate is negotiated or set. If the rate is set too low relative to the actual cost of providing care to the enrolled population, no amount of care management efficiency will produce a viable financial model. If the rate is set appropriately \u2014 reflecting the health acuity, demographic profile, and social complexity of the enrolled population \u2014 a well-managed capitated provider can generate margins of 3\u20138% while delivering care that is demonstrably better in quality and lower in total cost than the fee-for-service alternative. The actuarial process of setting a PMPM rate involves risk adjustment models that account for enrollee diagnoses, functional status, and social determinants of health, applied to utilization cost data from comparable populations. For Medicare Advantage plans, CMS sets the base rate using the county-level fee-for-service benchmark and adjusts it upward or downward based on each enrollee\u2019s Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) risk score, a diagnosis-based model that attempts to predict expected healthcare utilization for that individual in the coming year.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk018","_type":"block","style":"h2","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The Volume-to-Value Transition: Why the Math Gets Hard Before It Gets Easy","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk019","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The single most common financial mistake health systems make in VBC transitions is underestimating the revenue disruption of the transition period \u2014 the window, typically 18 to 36 months, during which care management investments have begun reducing utilization but VBC contract revenue has not yet scaled to replace the lost fee-for-service volume. Consider a regional health system generating $400 million in annual net patient revenue, with 30% of that revenue from inpatient admissions billed on a fee-for-service basis. The system joins MSSP and invests $2 million in care management infrastructure \u2014 care coordinators, a risk stratification platform, a post-discharge follow-up program \u2014 that begins generating measurable results in year one, reducing its attributed Medicare population\u2019s hospitalization rate by 12%. That 12% reduction represents approximately 240 avoided admissions. At an average net revenue of $8,500 per admission, it also represents a $2.04 million reduction in fee-for-service inpatient revenue. The system\u2019s MSSP shared savings payment for year one, based on total population savings, might be $1.4 million. Net financial impact of year one VBC investment: negative $640,000.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk020","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"This math is not an argument against VBC. It is an argument for understanding VBC as a multi-year financial investment with a specific payback horizon, rather than a year-one revenue enhancement strategy. The financial literature on mature ACO performance consistently shows that organizations reaching their fifth year of MSSP participation generate shared savings payments averaging $312 per attributed beneficiary annually, compared to an average investment cost of $87 per beneficiary in care management infrastructure \u2014 a return on investment of approximately 3.6 to 1. The problem is that most health system financial planning cycles operate on one-to-three year horizons, which are too short to capture the full economic benefit of VBC investment. Organizations that have successfully navigated the volume-to-value transition have done so by securing board approval for a five-to-seven year VBC investment thesis with explicit transition period loss projections, rather than attempting to justify each year\u2019s VBC expenditure against that same year\u2019s VBC revenue.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk021","_type":"block","style":"callout","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"For CFOs and Finance Leaders: If your organization is evaluating ACO or Advanced APM participation, your financial model must explicitly project the transition period revenue displacement \u2014 the reduction in fee-for-service inpatient and ED revenue that will occur as care management succeeds. An ACO financial model that shows positive net revenue in year one almost certainly has a methodology error, either in the care management cost estimates or in the assumed savings rate. Realistic five-year models typically show a cumulative loss in years one and two, breakeven in year three, and meaningful positive return in years four and five. Present this model honestly to your board, or the VBC investment will be defunded the first time a quarterly loss appears.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk022","_type":"block","style":"h2","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Primary Care Investment as Economic Infrastructure","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk023","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"One of the most powerful and counterintuitive findings in health economics is that investment in primary care produces returns that are comparable to, and in many cases superior to, investment in specialty care infrastructure \u2014 not in terms of individual clinical case intensity, but in terms of total population health spending and outcomes. The economic mechanism is straightforward once articulated: primary care reduces the incidence of the expensive downstream events \u2014 hospitalizations, emergency visits, specialist procedures, complications of uncontrolled chronic disease \u2014 that account for the vast majority of total healthcare spending. A study published in Health Affairs in 2024 analyzing Medicare spending patterns across 306 hospital referral regions found that regions with above-median primary care physician supply had 11.2% lower total Medicare spending per beneficiary, 18.4% fewer preventable hospital admissions, and 14.7% lower 30-day readmission rates than regions with below-median primary care supply, after controlling for demographic and health status differences.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk024","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The economic return on primary care investment is particularly relevant for value-based care organizations making resource allocation decisions. Under fee-for-service, a hospital has limited financial incentive to invest in expanding primary care capacity in its community \u2014 more primary care visits may mean fewer specialist referrals and fewer hospitalizations, which means less hospital revenue. Under a capitated or shared savings VBC model, the same investment in primary care capacity is a direct cost reduction strategy: every diabetic patient who sees their primary care provider quarterly and maintains target HbA1c levels is a patient who is unlikely to generate an $18,000 diabetic complication admission. The VBC payment model converts primary care from a cost center competing with hospital services for capital allocation into a return-generating infrastructure investment \u2014 which is the single       "hint": "Think about what aggregate statistics can hide.",
      "answer": "Not without disaggregating the data.       "question": "A community health worker in your organization reports that a risk stratification algorithm has been flagging very few Black patients on her panel for high-intensity care management — even patients she knows from clinical experience to be at high risk. What should she do, and what structural issue does this reflect?",
      "hint": "Think about the 2019 Science study and how AI models are trained.",
      "answer": "The CHW should escalate her observation to clinical and data analytics leadership as a potential algorithmic bias issue — this is exactly the kind of frontline signal that formal AI equity audits are designed to detect. The structural issue is that AI risk stratification models are trained on historical utilization data, and if Black patients in the training dataset historically had lower healthcare utilization due to access barriers — not because they were healthier — the model will have learned to associate lower utilization with lower risk, systematically underestimating the risk of Black patients. This is the bias mechanism identified in the 2019 Obermeyer et al. Science study. The organization should conduct a formal demographic equity audit of the algorithm and report findings to leadership. If the bias is confirmed, the tool must be recalibrated, replaced, or supplemented with clinical judgment for affected populations."

The result is a regulatory environment of extraordinary complexity that can simultaneously protect patients and obstruct innovation, often in the same rule. MACRA was passed with rare bipartisan consensus, repealing the deeply unpopular Sustainable Growth Rate formula that had governed Medicare physician payments since 1997 and replacing it with a two-track system that explicitly links physician payment updates to VBC participation. MIPS is designed as a transitional step \u2014 it maintains the fee-for-service base payment structure while adding a performance overlay that rewards quality and penalizes inefficiency. The alternative track, and the one that MACRA\u2019s architects intended as the destination, is participation in an Advanced Alternative Payment Model, or APM, which includes CMS-approved VBC arrangements that meet specific risk and quality criteria. {"_type":"academyModule","title":"Value-Based Care Fundamentals \u2014 Module 4: The Technology Pillar \u2014 Data, AI, and the Digital Infrastructure That Makes VBC Work","slug":{"current":"vbc-fundamentals-module-4-technology-pillar"},"publishedAt":"2026-03-07T10:00:00Z","pillar":"Technology","summary":"Module 4 of the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course examines the technology infrastructure that value-based care requires to function \u2014 and what happens when that infrastructure is missing. This module explains, in plain language, what interoperable electronic health records, health information exchange, and AI-powered risk stratification tools actually do in a VBC context, why 34% of rural Critical Access Hospitals remain technology-unready for advanced VBC participation, and how the federal interoperability agenda \u2014 including the 21st Century Cures Act, the CMS Interoperability Rule, and the TEFCA framework \u2014 is building the data infrastructure that VBC depends upon. Connecting passengers to flights would be technically possible but operationally chaotic \u2014 delays, lost records, missed connections, and dangerous errors would be routine, not exceptional. This is, only slightly exaggerated, the state of health information exchange in the United States as recently as 2019, and in many rural markets as recently as 2024. Value-based care requires something that American healthcare has never had at scale: a reliable, real-time, standards-based system for sharing patient health information across organizational boundaries. Without it, an Accountable Care Organization cannot know that its attributed Medicare patient was admitted to a hospital outside the network last Tuesday. A care coordinator cannot know that a high-risk patient missed their primary care appointment. A risk stratification algorithm cannot identify a patient approaching a high-cost event without complete longitudinal data about their diagnosis history, medication adherence, and recent utilization. Technology is not a nice-to-have for advanced VBC. It is the operating system on which the entire model runs.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk002","_type":"block","style":"h2","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The Three Technology Layers VBC Requires","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk003","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The technology infrastructure that supports effective value-based care can be understood as three interdependent layers, each building on the one below it. The foundation layer is clinical data capture: the electronic health record system that documents every patient encounter, diagnosis, medication, order, and result in a structured, machine-readable format. The second layer is data integration and exchange: the health information exchange infrastructure that connects EHR systems across organizations so that complete patient data is available regardless of where care was delivered. The third layer is analytics and intelligence: the population health management platforms, risk stratification tools, and increasingly AI-powered predictive models that transform raw clinical data into actionable care management intelligence \u2014 identifying which patients are at highest risk of imminent high-cost events, which chronic disease patients are overdue for interventions, and which populations are generating the most preventable utilization. Each layer is necessary but not sufficient. Strong EHR implementation without HIE connectivity produces siloed data. HIE connectivity without analytics produces data that no one has the capacity to act on. Analytics without high-quality underlying data produces predictions that are wrong in ways that are hard to detect until they cause harm.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk004","_type":"block","style":"h2","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Electronic Health Records: The Foundation Layer","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk005","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The United States made a massive federal investment in EHR adoption through the HITECH Act of 2009, which appropriated $27 billion in Medicare and Medicaid incentive payments to encourage providers to implement certified EHR systems and demonstrate \u201cmeaningful use\u201d \u2014 a defined set of capabilities including electronic prescribing, clinical decision support, and patient portal access. By 2021, 88% of hospitals and 78% of office-based physicians had implemented certified EHR systems, a transformation from the 9% hospital adoption rate that existed in 2008. This is one of the most rapid technology adoption curves in the history of any industry, and it created the clinical data foundation that value-based care analytics requires. However, EHR adoption rates mask significant quality variation that is directly relevant to VBC capability. Having a certified EHR does not mean having a fully configured, fully utilized EHR that generates high-quality structured data. This provision was specifically designed to address a well-documented pattern in which EHR vendors and some health systems restricted data sharing with competitors or external partners, creating artificial data silos that served commercial interests at the expense of care coordination. Second, it mandated that all certified EHR systems implement standardized FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) application programming interfaces by 2022, enabling third-party developers to build population health applications that connect directly to EHR data without requiring custom integrations. The FHIR mandate is the technical foundation of the modern population health analytics market, as it allows risk stratification platforms, care gap tools, and quality reporting systems to access EHR data through a single standardized connection rather than a patchwork of proprietary integrations.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk009","_type":"block","style":"quote","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The 21st Century Cures Act\u2019s information blocking prohibition changed the competitive dynamics of health IT in a way that CMS\u2019s interoperability rules alone could not have. In a VBC model managing 10,000 attributed patients, a care management team cannot proactively reach out to every patient every month. They need a system that identifies the 300 or 400 patients most likely to have a preventable hospital admission, emergency department visit, or serious clinical deterioration in the next 90 days, so that care coordination resources can be concentrated where they will have the greatest impact. Traditional risk stratification relied on simple actuarial models \u2014 patients with the highest total spending in the prior year were assumed to be the highest risk in the coming year. These models are easy to implement but systematically misdirected: they identify patients who were recently sick rather than patients who are about to become sick, missing the early intervention window where care management is most effective and most cost-efficient.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk017","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"Modern AI-powered risk stratification uses machine learning models trained on large clinical datasets to predict future utilization risk based on a much richer set of signals than historical spending alone. These models incorporate diagnosis trajectories (the sequence and pattern of diagnoses over time, not just their presence or absence), medication adherence signals derived from pharmacy data and EHR medication reconciliation records, laboratory value trends (a gradually rising HbA1c over three visits is a stronger predictor of near-term hospitalization than a single elevated value), social determinants of health flags derived from screening questionnaires and zip-code-level data, and behavioral health diagnoses and substance use disorder flags that are strongly predictive of high-cost medical utilization. The predictive accuracy of leading AI risk stratification models, as measured by the C-statistic \u2014 the probability that the model correctly identifies a patient who will be hospitalized as higher risk than a patient who will not \u2014 has improved from approximately 0.70 for traditional claims-based models to 0.82\u20130.87 for the leading AI models that incorporate multi-modal EHR data, a meaningful improvement that translates directly into better care management targeting and higher ROI on care coordinator time.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk018","_type":"block","style":"h3","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The AI Bias Problem: When Risk Stratification Perpetuates Inequity","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk019","_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"AI risk stratification tools carry a well-documented and serious equity risk: because they are trained on historical healthcare utilization data, they tend to encode the biases present in that data. The algorithm learned that low-cost patients were low-need patients, a correlation that held for white patients but produced systematic underestimation of Black patients\u2019 clinical risk. The practical consequence was that Black patients were significantly less likely to be identified for high-intensity care management programs, perpetuating the very care access disparities that VBC is intended to address. This finding has been replicated for other demographic groups and other algorithm types, establishing AI bias as a genuine and important equity challenge in VBC technology deployment.","marks":[]}]},{"_key":"blk019b","_type":"block","style":"quote","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"We audited five commercial risk stratification products used by our ACO network and found that four of them showed statistically significant underestimation of risk for patients in the lowest income quintile. What VBC requires is reliable clinical data capture, standards-based data exchange, and analytics capable of turning population data into actionable care management intelligence. These are not science-fiction capabilities. They exist today in mature form at health systems like Kaiser Permanente, Intermountain Healthcare, and Geisinger. The challenge is not invention \u2014 it is diffusion. The 34% of rural Critical Access Hospitals that lack the foundational technology capabilities for advanced VBC participation are not being held back by the absence of technology. File: frontend/sanity/generate_sanity_content.py

import json
import os
import google.generativeai as genai
from dotenv import load_dotenv

# Load environment variables from .env file
load_dotenv()

# Initialize Gemini client
GOOGLE_API_KEY = os.getenv("GOOGLE_API_KEY")
if not GOOGLE_API_KEY:
    raise ValueError("GOOGLE_API_KEY is required in your .env file")

genai.configure(api_key=GOOGLE_API_KEY)
model = genai.GenerativeModel(
    model_name="gemini-2.0-flash",
    generation_config=genai.GenerationConfig(
        response_mime_type="application/json",
        temperature=0.7,
    ),
    system_instruction="You are a CMS JSON generator. Always respond with valid JSON only.",
)


def generate_sanity_article(topic, data_points):
    """
    Generates a Sanity-compatible JSON article using Gemini and a prompt template.
    """

    # 1. Define Paths
    base_path = os.getcwd()
    template_path = "frontend/sanity/prompt_template_v10.txt"

    if base_path.endswith("backend") or not os.path.exists(template_path):
        if os.path.exists("../frontend/sanity/prompt_template_v10.txt"):
            template_path = "../frontend/sanity/prompt_template_v10.txt"

    if not os.path.exists(template_path):
        print(f"❌ Error: Template file not found at {template_path}")
        print(f"Current working directory: {base_path}")
        return

    # 2. Load the Template
    with open(template_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        prompt_content = f.read()

    # 3. Inject Variables
    final_prompt = prompt_content.replace("[Insert Topic]", topic)
    final_prompt = final_prompt.replace("[Insert Data]", data_points)

    # 4. Call Gemini with JSON enforcement
    print(f"Generating article for: {topic}...")

    try:
        response = model.generate_content(final_prompt)
        raw_content = response.text
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"❌ Gemini API Error: {e}")
        return

    # 5. Extract and Validate
    try:
        article_json = json.loads(raw_content)

        output_dir = "frontend/sanity/content"
        if template_path.startswith(".."):
            output_dir = "../frontend/sanity/content"

        os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)

        slug = article_json.get("slug", {}).get("current", "untitled-article")
        filename = os.path.join(output_dir, f"{slug}.json")

        with open(filename, "w", encoding="utf-8") as out:
            json.dump(article_json, out, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)

        print(f"✅ Success! Saved to {filename}")
        return article_json

    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        print("❌ Error: Gemini did not output valid JSON.")
        print("Raw Output:", raw_content)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"❌ Error saving file: {e}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("--- Sanity Content Generator (Gemini) ---")
    topic_in = input("Enter Topic: ") or "The Impact of AI on Rural Health"
    data_in = input("Enter Key Data: ") or "Cost reduction: 15%, Efficiency: +20%"

    generate_sanity_article(topic_in, data_in)

// scripts/import_academy.js
// Usage: node scripts/import_academy.js <filename.json>
// File must exist inside sanity/content/academy/

const { createClient } = require("@sanity/client");
const path = require("path");
const fs = require("fs");

require("dotenv").config({ path: path.resolve(__dirname, "../.env.local") });

// ── Env validation ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
const { SANITY_API_TOKEN, NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID, NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET } = process.env;

if (!SANITY_API_TOKEN) {
  console.error("❌ SANITY_API_TOKEN is missing from .env.local");
  process.exit(1);
}
if (!NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID) {
  console.error("❌ NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID is missing from .env.local");
  process.exit(1);
}

// ── Sanity client ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
const client = createClient({
  projectId: NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID,
  dataset: NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET || "production",
  token: SANITY_API_TOKEN,
  apiVersion: "2024-01-01",
  useCdn: false,
});

// ── Argument parsing ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
const [filename] = process.argv.slice(2);
if (!filename) {
  console.error("❌ Usage: node scripts/import_academy.js <filename.json>");
  console.error("   File must exist inside: sanity/content/academy/");
  process.exit(1);
}

const CONTENT_DIR = path.resolve(__dirname, "../sanity/content/academy");
const filePath = path.join(CONTENT_DIR, filename);

// ── Constants ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
const REQUIRED_FIELDS = ["title", "slug", "courseTitle", "moduleNumber", "summary", "body"];
const VALID_PILLARS   = ["Policy", "Economics", "Technology", "Clinical", "Equity", "All"];
const VALID_LEVELS    = ["Foundational", "Intermediate", "Advanced"];
const MIN_BODY_BLOCKS = 35;

// ── Sanitize body ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// Must run BEFORE validation so checks operate on clean data.
//
// Two things to fix in AI-generated content:
//   1. Missing _key on blocks/children (Sanity requires unique keys on all array items)
//   2. `code` blocks where AI emits an array of objects instead of a string.
//      Sanity attribute names must match /^\$?[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$/ — human-readable
//      keys like "Typical U.S. Adoption" are rejected. Serialize to JSON string.
const rk = () => Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10);

// Ensure _key on every item in an array of objects
function keyed(arr) {
  if (!Array.isArray(arr)) return arr;
  return arr.map((item) => ({ ...item, _key: item._key || rk() }));
}

function sanitizeBody(body) {
  return body.map((block) => {
    if (!block._key) block._key = rk();

    switch (block._type) {
      // Legacy data table: code field as array → stringify to JSON
      case "code":
        if (Array.isArray(block.code)) {
          block.code = JSON.stringify(block.code, null, 2);
          if (!block.language) block.language = "json";
        }
        break;

      // Standard rich text — ensure child spans have _key
      case "block":
        if (Array.isArray(block.children)) {
          block.children = block.children.map((c) => ({ ...c, _key: c._key || rk() }));
        }
        break;

      // Educational block types — ensure nested array items have _key
      case "statGrid":
        block.stats = keyed(block.stats);
        break;
      case "comparisonBlock":
        block.rows = keyed(block.rows);
        break;
      case "stepBlock":
        block.steps = keyed(block.steps);
        break;
    }

    return block;
  });
}

// ── Validation ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
function validate(data) {
  const errors = [];

  for (const field of REQUIRED_FIELDS) {
    if (!data[field]) errors.push(`Missing required field: "${field}"`);
  }

  if (data.pillar && !VALID_PILLARS.includes(data.pillar)) {
    errors.push(`Invalid pillar "${data.pillar}". Must be one of: ${VALID_PILLARS.join(", ")}`);
  }

  if (data.level && !VALID_LEVELS.includes(data.level)) {
    errors.push(`Invalid level "${data.level}". Must be one of: ${VALID_LEVELS.join(", ")}`);
  }

  if (!Array.isArray(data.body) || data.body.length < MIN_BODY_BLOCKS) {
    errors.push(
      `Body must have at least ${MIN_BODY_BLOCKS} blocks (found ${
        Array.isArray(data.body) ? data.body.length : 0
      })`
    );
  }

  if (Array.isArray(data.body)) {
    const keys = data.body.map((b) => b._key);
    if (new Set(keys).size !== keys.length) {
      errors.push("Body blocks contain duplicate _key values");
    }
  }

  return errors;
}

// ── Main ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
async function run() {
  if (!fs.existsSync(filePath)) {
    console.error(`❌ File not found: ${filePath}`);
    process.exit(1);
  }

  let moduleData;
  try {
    moduleData = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(filePath, "utf8"));
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(`❌ Invalid JSON in ${filename}: ${err.message}`);
    process.exit(1);
  }

  moduleData._type = "academyModule";

  if (Array.isArray(moduleData.body)) {
    moduleData.body = sanitizeBody(moduleData.body);
  }

  const errors = validate(moduleData);
  if (errors.length > 0) {
    console.error("❌ Validation failed:");
    errors.forEach((e) => console.error(`   • ${e}`));
    process.exit(1);
  }

  console.log(`🎓 Importing: "${moduleData.title}"`);
  console.log(`   Course  : ${moduleData.courseTitle}`);
  console.log(`   Module# : ${moduleData.moduleNumber}`);
  console.log(`   Pillar  : ${moduleData.pillar || "not set"}`);
  console.log(`   Blocks  : ${moduleData.body.length}`);

  try {
    // createOrReplace is atomic and idempotent — safe to re-run without data loss.
    // delete+create is not: if create fails, the document is already gone.
    const docId = `academyModule-${moduleData.slug.current}`;
    const result = await client.createOrReplace({ _id: docId, ...moduleData });
    console.log(`✅ Imported. Sanity ID: ${result._id}`);
    console.log(`   Preview: /academy/modules/${moduleData.slug.current}`);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(`❌ Sanity error: ${err.message}`);
    if (err.message.includes("Insufficient permissions")) {
      console.error("   → Check that your token has Editor permissions.");
    }
    process.exit(1);
  }
}

run();

File: frontend/scripts/seed-content.ts

#!/usr/bin/env npx tsx
/**
 * scripts/seed-content.ts
 *
 * Seeds editorial content across all five pillars:
 *   - policyAnalysis  (5 per pillar = 25 total)
 *   - academyModule   (2 courses × 3 modules = 6 modules)
 *   - definition      (30 glossary terms)
 *   - caseStudy       (5 total)
 *   - analystNote     (5 sidebar notes)
 *
 * Usage:
 *   npx tsx scripts/seed-content.ts
 *
 * Prerequisites:
 *   - SANITY_API_TOKEN (write token) in .env.local or shell env
 *   - NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID and NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET must be set
 */

import * as dotenv from "dotenv";
import * as path from "path";
dotenv.config({ path: path.resolve(__dirname, "../.env.local") });

import { createClient } from "@sanity/client";

const sanity = createClient({
  projectId: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID!,
  dataset: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET || "production",
  apiVersion: "2024-01-01",
  token: process.env.SANITY_API_TOKEN,
  useCdn: false,
});

// ── Portable Text helpers ────────────────────────────────────────────────────

let keyCounter = 0;
const k = () => `k${++keyCounter}`;

function para(text: string) {
  return {
    _type: "block",
    _key: k(),
    style: "normal",
    children: [{ _type: "span", _key: k(), text, marks: [] }],
    markDefs: [],
  };
}

function h2(text: string) {
  return {
    _type: "block",
    _key: k(),
    style: "h2",
    children: [{ _type: "span", _key: k(), text, marks: [] }],
    markDefs: [],
  };
}

function h3(text: string) {
  return {
    _type: "block",
    _key: k(),
    style: "h3",
    children: [{ _type: "span", _key: k(), text, marks: [] }],
    markDefs: [],
  };
}

function slug(s: string) {
  return { _type: "slug", current: s };
}

function dt(year: number, month: number, day: number) {
  return new Date(year, month - 1, day).toISOString();
}

      ),

If denied, Vermont faces a structural deficit that could force program rollback before 2028 implementation. This is the most consequential state health policy experiment of 2026."
    ),
    author: "HTR Policy Intelligence",
  },
];

// ── Seeding Functions ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

async function seedCollection(name: string, docs: Record<string, unknown>[]) {
  console.log(`\nSeeding ${docs.length} ${name}…`);
  let succeeded = 0;
  for (const doc of docs) {
    try {
      await sanity.createOrReplace(doc as Parameters<typeof sanity.createOrReplace>[0]);
      console.log(`  ✓ ${(doc.title ?? doc.headline ?? doc.term ?? doc._id) as string}`);
      succeeded++;
    } catch (err) {
      console.error(`  ✗ ${doc._id}: ${err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)}`);
    }
  }
  console.log(`  ${succeeded}/${docs.length} seeded successfully.`);
}

async function main() {
  console.log("Vermont Health Platform — Content Seed Script");
  console.log("==============================================");
  console.log(`Project: ${process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID}`);
  console.log(`Dataset: ${process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET || "production"}\n`);

  await seedCollection("policyAnalysis documents", policyAnalyses);
  await seedCollection("academyModule documents", academyModules);
  await seedCollection("definition documents", definitions.map((d, i) => ({
    _id: `definition-${String(i + 1).padStart(3, "0")}`,
    _type: "definition",
    term: d.term,
    description: d.description,
    pillars: d.pillars,
  })));
  await seedCollection("caseStudy documents", caseStudies);
  await seedCollection("analystNote documents", analystNotes);

  console.log("\n==============================================");
  console.log("Seed complete. Summary:");
  console.log(`  Policy Analyses: ${policyAnalyses.length}`);
  console.log(`  Academy Modules: ${academyModules.length}`);
  console.log(`  Definitions:     ${definitions.length}`);
  console.log(`  Case Studies:    ${caseStudies.length}`);
  console.log(`  Analyst Notes:   ${analystNotes.length}`);
  console.log(`  TOTAL:           ${policyAnalyses.length + academyModules.length + definitions.length + caseStudies.length + analystNotes.length} documents`);
}

main().catch((err) => {
  console.error(err);
  process.exit(1);
});

#!/usr/bin/env npx tsx
/**
 * scripts/seed-hospitals.ts
 *
 * Seeds hospital documents in Sanity from the static hospital-data.ts file.
 * Run once to migrate; after that, edit hospitals in the Sanity Studio.
 *
 * Usage:
 *   npx tsx scripts/seed-hospitals.ts
 *
 * Prerequisites:
 *   - SANITY_API_TOKEN (write token) in .env.local or shell env
 *   - NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID and NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET must be set
 */

import * as dotenv from "dotenv";
import * as path from "path";
dotenv.config({ path: path.resolve(__dirname, "../.env.local") });

import { createClient } from "@sanity/client";
import { hospitalData } from "../lib/data/hospital-data";

const sanity = createClient({
  projectId: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID!,
  dataset: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET || "production",
  apiVersion: "2024-01-01",
  token: process.env.SANITY_API_TOKEN,
  useCdn: false,
});

async function main() {
  const allEntries = Object.entries(hospitalData);
  const totalHospitals = allEntries.reduce((acc, [, h]) => acc + h.length, 0);

  console.log(`Seeding ${totalHospitals} hospital documents across ${allEntries.length} states…`);

  let succeeded = 0;
  for (const [stateSlug, hospitals] of allEntries) {
    for (const h of hospitals) {
      const doc = {
        _id: `hospital-${h.id}`,
        _type: "hospital",
        name: h.name,
        stateSlug,
        city: h.city,
        type: h.type,
        totalDischarges: h.totalDischarges,
        avgLengthOfStay: h.avgLengthOfStay,
        qualityScore: h.qualityScore,
      };
      try {
        await sanity.createOrReplace(doc);
        console.log(`  ✓ [${stateSlug}] ${h.name}`);
        succeeded++;
      } catch (err) {
        console.error(`  ✗ [${stateSlug}] ${h.name}: ${err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)}`);
      }
    }
  }

  console.log(`\nDone. ${succeeded}/${totalHospitals} hospitals seeded.`);
}

main().catch((err) => {
  console.error(err);
  process.exit(1);
});

#!/usr/bin/env npx tsx
/**
 * scripts/sync-embeddings.ts
 *
 * Syncs HTR content from Sanity → Supabase pgvector.
 * Run once initially, then whenever content is updated.
 *
 * Usage:
 *   npx tsx scripts/sync-embeddings.ts
 *
 * Prerequisites:
 *   - Run supabase/setup-rag.sql in the Supabase dashboard first.
 *   - Ensure .env.local has GEMINI_API_KEY, SANITY_API_TOKEN,
 *     NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID, NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL,
 *     SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY.
 */

import * as dotenv from "dotenv";
import path from "path";

// Load .env.local from the frontend directory
dotenv.config({ path: path.resolve(__dirname, "../.env.local") });

import { createClient as createSanityClient } from "@sanity/client";
import { createClient as createSupabaseClient } from "@supabase/supabase-js";
import { GoogleGenerativeAI } from "@google/generative-ai";

// ── Clients ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

const sanity = createSanityClient({
  projectId: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID!,
  dataset: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET || "production",
  apiVersion: "2023-10-01",
  token: process.env.SANITY_API_TOKEN,
  useCdn: false,
});

// Use service role key so we can write to Supabase (bypasses RLS)
const supabase = createSupabaseClient(
  process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL!,
  process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY!
);

const genAI = new GoogleGenerativeAI(process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY!);
const embeddingModel = genAI.getGenerativeModel({ model: "text-embedding-004" });

// ── Helpers ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

/** Extract plain text from Sanity Portable Text blocks. */
function portableTextToPlain(blocks: unknown): string {
  if (!Array.isArray(blocks)) return "";
  type PTBlock = { _type?: string; children?: Array<{ text?: string }> };
  return (blocks as PTBlock[])
    .filter((b): b is PTBlock & { children: Array<{ text?: string }> } =>
      b._type === "block" && Array.isArray(b.children)
    )
    .map((b) =>
      b.children
        .filter((span) => typeof span.text === "string")
        .map((span) => span.text)
        .join("")
    )
    .join("\n");
}

/** Safely extract slug.current from an unknown Sanity slug field. */
function slugCurrent(slug: unknown): string | undefined {
  if (slug && typeof slug === "object" && "current" in slug) {
    return (slug as { current?: string }).current;
  }
  return undefined;
}

/** Truncate text to stay within embedding API limits. */
function truncate(text: string, maxChars = 8000): string {
  return text.length > maxChars ? text.slice(0, maxChars) : text;
}

async function embed(text: string): Promise<number[]> {
  const result = await embeddingModel.embedContent(truncate(text));
  return result.embedding.values;
}

/** Rate-limit: small delay between embedding API calls. */
function sleep(ms: number) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
}

// ── Content extractors ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

interface ContentRecord {
  content_id: string;
  content_type: string;
  title: string | null;
  content: string;
  url: string | null;
  pillar: string | null;
}

async function fetchPolicyAnalyses(): Promise<ContentRecord[]> {
  const docs = await sanity.fetch(`
    *[_type == "policyAnalysis" && defined(slug.current)]{
      _id, title, slug, pillar, summary, body
    }
  `);
  return docs.map((d: Record<string, unknown>) => {
    const bodyText = portableTextToPlain(d.body ?? []);
    const content = [d.summary, bodyText].filter(Boolean).join("\n\n");
    const pillarSlug = String(d.pillar ?? "").toLowerCase();
    return {
      content_id: d._id,
      content_type: "policyAnalysis",
      title: d.title ?? null,
      content: truncate(content),
      url: `/${pillarSlug}/${slugCurrent(d.slug)}`,
      pillar: d.pillar ?? null,
    };
  });
}

async function fetchPosts(): Promise<ContentRecord[]> {
  const docs = await sanity.fetch(`
    *[_type == "post" && defined(slug.current)]{
      _id, title, slug, body
    }
  `);
  return docs.map((d: Record<string, unknown>) => ({
    content_id: d._id,
    content_type: "post",
    title: d.title ?? null,
    content: truncate(portableTextToPlain(d.body ?? [])),
    url: `/post/${slugCurrent(d.slug)}`,
    pillar: null,
  }));
}

async function fetchAcademyModules(): Promise<ContentRecord[]> {
  const docs = await sanity.fetch(`
    *[_type == "academyModule" && defined(slug.current)]{
      _id, title, slug, pillar, summary, learningObjectives, body
    }
  `);
  return docs.map((d: Record<string, unknown>) => {
    const objectives = Array.isArray(d.learningObjectives)
      ? d.learningObjectives.join(". ")
      : "";
    const bodyText = portableTextToPlain(d.body ?? []);
    const content = [d.summary, objectives, bodyText]
      .filter(Boolean)
      .join("\n\n");
    return {
      content_id: d._id,
      content_type: "academyModule",
      title: d.title ?? null,
      content: truncate(content),
      url: `/academy/modules/${slugCurrent(d.slug)}`,
      pillar: d.pillar ?? null,
    };
  });
}

async function fetchCaseStudies(): Promise<ContentRecord[]> {
  const docs = await sanity.fetch(`
    *[_type == "caseStudy" && defined(slug.current)]{
      _id, title, slug, pillar, body
    }
  `);
  return docs.map((d: Record<string, unknown>) => ({
    content_id: d._id,
    content_type: "caseStudy",
    title: d.title ?? null,
    content: truncate(portableTextToPlain(d.body ?? [])),
    url: `/academy/case-studies/${slugCurrent(d.slug)}`,
    pillar: d.pillar ?? null,
  }));
}

async function fetchDefinitions(): Promise<ContentRecord[]> {
  const docs = await sanity.fetch(`
    *[_type == "definition"]{
      _id, term, description, pillars
    }
  `);
  return docs.map((d: Record<string, unknown>) => ({
    content_id: d._id,
    content_type: "definition",
    title: d.term ?? null,
    content: truncate(`${d.term}: ${d.description ?? ""}`),
    url: `/academy/glossary`,
    pillar: Array.isArray(d.pillars) ? d.pillars[0] ?? null : null,
  }));
}

async function fetchAnalystNotes(): Promise<ContentRecord[]> {
  const docs = await sanity.fetch(`
    *[_type == "analystNote"]{
      _id, title, pillar, body
    }
  `);
  return docs.map((d: Record<string, unknown>) => ({
    content_id: d._id,
    content_type: "analystNote",
    title: d.title ?? null,
    content: truncate(portableTextToPlain(d.body ?? [])),
    url: null,
    pillar: d.pillar ?? null,
  }));
}

async function fetchWebinars(): Promise<ContentRecord[]> {
  const docs = await sanity.fetch(`
    *[_type == "webinar" && defined(slug.current)]{
      _id, title, slug, pillar, description
    }
  `);
  return docs.map((d: Record<string, unknown>) => ({
    content_id: d._id,
    content_type: "webinar",
    title: d.title ?? null,
    content: truncate(`${d.title ?? ""}\n${d.description ?? ""}`),
    url: `/academy/webinars/${slugCurrent(d.slug)}`,
    pillar: d.pillar ?? null,
  }));
}

async function fetchReports(): Promise<ContentRecord[]> {
  const docs = await sanity.fetch(`
    *[_type == "report" && defined(slug.current)]{
      _id, title, slug, pillar, abstract
    }
  `);
  return docs.map((d: Record<string, unknown>) => ({
    content_id: d._id,
    content_type: "report",
    title: d.title ?? null,
    content: truncate(`${d.title ?? ""}\n${d.abstract ?? ""}`),
    url: `/report/${slugCurrent(d.slug)}`,
    pillar: d.pillar ?? null,
  }));
}

// ── Main sync ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

async function syncAll() {
  console.log("Fetching content from Sanity...");

  const allRecords: ContentRecord[] = [
    ...(await fetchPolicyAnalyses()),
    ...(await fetchPosts()),
    ...(await fetchAcademyModules()),
    ...(await fetchCaseStudies()),
    ...(await fetchDefinitions()),
    ...(await fetchAnalystNotes()),
    ...(await fetchWebinars()),
    ...(await fetchReports()),
  ].filter((r) => r.content.trim().length > 20); // Skip near-empty docs

  console.log(`Found ${allRecords.length} documents to embed.`);

  let synced = 0;
  let skipped = 0;
  let errors = 0;

  for (const record of allRecords) {
    try {
      const embedding = await embed(record.content);

      const { error } = await supabase
        .from("content_embeddings")
        .upsert(
          {
            content_id: record.content_id,
            content_type: record.content_type,
            title: record.title,
            content: record.content,
            url: record.url,
            pillar: record.pillar,
            embedding,
            updated_at: new Date().toISOString(),
          },
          { onConflict: "content_id" }
        );

      if (error) {
        console.error(`  ✗ ${record.content_id}: ${error.message}`);
        errors++;
      } else {
        console.log(`  ✓ [${record.content_type}] ${record.title ?? record.content_id}`);
        synced++;
      }

      // Stay within Gemini free-tier rate limits (~60 req/min)
      await sleep(1000);
    } catch (err) {
      console.error(`  ✗ ${record.content_id}: ${err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)}`);
      errors++;
      await sleep(2000); // Back off on errors
    }
  }

  console.log(`\nDone. ${synced} synced, ${skipped} skipped, ${errors} errors.`);
}

syncAll().catch((err) => {
  console.error("Fatal error:", err);
  process.exit(1);
});

"use client";

import React, { useState } from "react";

interface TickerItem {
  label: string;
  value: string;
  trend: string;
  status: string;
}

export default function TickerStrip({ tickerData }: { tickerData: TickerItem[] }) {
  const [isPaused, setIsPaused] = useState(false);
  const [isHidden, setIsHidden] = useState(false);

  const getTickerColor = (status: string) => {
    switch (status) {
      case 'good': return 'text-emerald-700';
      case 'warning': return 'text-orange-600';
      case 'critical': return 'text-rose-600';
      default: return 'text-indigo-600';
    }
  };

  return (
    <div className="w-full bg-white transition-all duration-300">
      
      {/* --- CONTROLS ROW --- */}
      {/* Responsive: Hidden on mobile (hidden), Flex on desktop (md:flex) */}
      {/* Layout: Standard Flexbox centering */}
      {/* Padding: Standard minimal padding (py-1) */}
      <div className="hidden md:flex container mx-auto px-4 justify-end items-center gap-4 border-b border-slate-100 py-1">
        
        {/* 1. PAUSE CONTROL */}
        {!isHidden && (
            <>
                <label className="flex items-center gap-1.5 cursor-pointer group select-none">
                    <input 
                        type="checkbox" 
                        checked={isPaused} 
                        onChange={(e) => setIsPaused(e.target.checked)}
                        className="w-3 h-3 text-indigo-600 rounded border-slate-300 focus:ring-indigo-500 cursor-pointer"
                    />
                    <span className="text-[10px] font-bold text-slate-400 group-hover:text-slate-600 uppercase tracking-wider transition-colors">
                        Pause Ticker
                    </span>
                </label>
                {/* Separator Line */}
                <div className="h-3 w-px bg-slate-200"></div>
            </>
        )}

        {/* 2. SHOW/HIDE CONTROL */}
        <label className="flex items-center gap-1.5 cursor-pointer group select-none">
            <input 
                type="checkbox" 
                checked={isHidden} 
                onChange={(e) => {
                    setIsHidden(e.target.checked);
                    if (e.target.checked) setIsPaused(false); 
                }}
                className="w-3 h-3 text-indigo-600 rounded border-slate-300 focus:ring-indigo-500 cursor-pointer"
            />
            <span className="text-[10px] font-bold text-slate-400 group-hover:text-slate-600 uppercase tracking-wider transition-colors">
                {isHidden ? "Show Ticker" : "Hide Ticker"}
            </span>
        </label>
      </div>

      {/* --- TICKER ROW --- */}
      <div 
        className={`bg-slate-50 border-b border-slate-200 flex items-center overflow-hidden w-full transition-all duration-500 ease-in-out ${isHidden ? 'h-0 opacity-0 border-none' : 'h-8 opacity-100'}`}
      >
        {!isHidden && (
            <>
                <div className="bg-slate-200 h-full flex items-center justify-center px-4 flex-shrink-0 z-10 border-r border-slate-300">
                    <span className="font-bold text-slate-700 uppercase tracking-widest text-[10px] whitespace-nowrap">
                        System Vitals
                    </span>
                </div>

                <div className="flex-1 overflow-hidden relative h-full mask-linear-fade">
                    <div 
                        className="flex items-center h-full animate-marquee whitespace-nowrap"
                        style={{ animationPlayState: isPaused ? 'paused' : 'running' }}
                    >
                        {tickerData.map((item, i) => (
                            <div key={`s1-${i}`} className="flex items-center gap-2 mx-8 whitespace-nowrap">
                                <span className="font-medium text-slate-500 text-xs">{item.label}:</span>
                                <span className={`font-bold text-xs ${getTickerColor(item.status)}`}>{item.value}</span> 
                                <span className="text-slate-400 text-[10px] uppercase">({item.trend})</span>
                            </div>
                        ))}
                        {tickerData.map((item, i) => (
                            <div key={`s2-${i}`} className="flex items-center gap-2 mx-8 whitespace-nowrap">
                                <span className="font-medium text-slate-500 text-xs">{item.label}:</span>
                                <span className={`font-bold text-xs ${getTickerColor(item.status)}`}>{item.value}</span> 
                                <span className="text-slate-400 text-[10px] uppercase">({item.trend})</span>
                            </div>
                        ))}
                        
                        {tickerData.length === 0 && (
                            <span className="mx-6 text-slate-400 text-xs italic">Connecting to HTR Index...</span>
                        )}
                    </div>
                </div>
            </>
        )}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

| UI Library | React | 19.0.0-rc | Pre-release — stable for production |
| Styling | Tailwind CSS | 4.0.0-beta.9 | v4 beta — uses `@theme` in CSS, not `tailwind.config.js` |
| Styled Components | styled-components | 6.3.8 | Used for a few legacy components only |
| CMS | Sanity | latest | Studio embedded at `/studio` route |
| CMS Client | next-sanity | latest | Includes `createClient` + live preview utilities |
| Database / Auth | Supabase | 2.89.0 | Postgres + pgvector + auth |
| Supabase SSR | @supabase/ssr | 0.9.0 | Server-side session handling in middleware |
| Maps | react-simple-maps | 1.0.0 | D3-backed SVG US map |
| Type Safety | TypeScript | 5.x | Strict mode enabled |
| Language | Node.js | 20.x | Dev and build environment |

### Backend AI Brain (Python)

| Layer | Technology | Version | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| API Framework | FastAPI | ≥0.111 | Async HTTP server; CORS configured for frontend |
| ASGI Server | uvicorn | ≥0.30 | Runs FastAPI; `--reload` flag for dev |
| AI Orchestration | LlamaIndex Core | ≥0.11 | VectorStoreIndex, ChatMemoryBuffer, streaming |
| LLM | Google Gemini Flash Lite | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | Via `llama-index-llms-google-genai` |
| Embedding Model | Google text-embedding-004 | — | 768-dim; via `llama-index-embeddings-google-genai` |
| PDF Ingestion | LlamaIndex SimpleDirectoryReader | — | Auto-discovers all `.pdf` files in `backend/data/` |
| HTTP Client | httpx | ≥0.27 | Async Sanity GROQ HTTP API calls |
| Vector Store | LlamaIndex in-memory + disk | — | Persisted to `backend/storage/` (gitignored) |

**Important version notes:**
- Next.js reports as `^16.1.6` in package.json — treat as Next.js 15 app router series.
- Tailwind v4 is a **breaking change** from v3: no `tailwind.config.js` theme extensions for custom colors — all color tokens live in `globals.css` via `@theme`.
- React 19 RC ships with concurrent features; no `ReactDOM.render()` — use `createRoot()`.
- The Python backend owns all AI logic. The Next.js `/api/chat` route is a **thin proxy** — it forwards requests to the Python backend and streams responses back. No AI logic lives in TypeScript.

## 3. Environment Variables

There are **two separate** `.env` files — one for the Next.js frontend, one for the Python backend.

### `frontend/.env.local` — Next.js app

Never commit this file.

```env
# ─── Sanity CMS ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Project ID and dataset from sanity.io/manage
NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID=your-project-id
NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET=production
NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_API_VERSION=2023-10-01

# Read/write API token for server-side mutations and seeding scripts.
# Generate at: sanity.io/manage → your project → API → Tokens
# Required permissions: Editor (or higher for mutations)
SANITY_API_TOKEN=your-sanity-api-token

# ─── Supabase ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Found in: Supabase dashboard → Project Settings → API
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=https://your-project-ref.supabase.co
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=your-anon-key

# Service role key — server-side only, bypasses Row Level Security.
# Used by sync-embeddings.ts (legacy RAG sync) to write to content_embeddings.
# NEVER expose to the browser.
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=your-service-role-key

# ─── Google AI (Embeddings — legacy sync script only) ────────────────────────
# Only needed if running sync-embeddings.ts (the legacy Supabase RAG sync).
# The AI Analyst chat itself no longer needs this key in the frontend —
# it proxies all AI calls to the Python backend.
GEMINI_API_KEY=your-gemini-api-key

# ─── Python AI Backend ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# URL of the running Python FastAPI backend.
# Default: http://localhost:8000 (used if this var is absent).
# Set to your production backend URL for deployment.
PYTHON_BACKEND_URL=http://localhost:8000
```

### `backend/.env` — Python AI Brain

Copy from `backend/.env.example` and fill in your values. Never commit this file.

```env
# ─── Google AI ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Powers Gemini LLM (gemini-flash-lite-latest) + embeddings (text-embedding-004)
# Get from: https://aistudio.google.com/app/apikey
GOOGLE_API_KEY=your-google-api-key

# ─── Sanity CMS ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# The Python backend fetches CMS content directly via GROQ HTTP API.
# Use a read-only API token (no write permissions needed).
SANITY_PROJECT_ID=your-project-id
SANITY_DATASET=production
SANITY_API_TOKEN=your-read-only-sanity-token
SANITY_API_VERSION=2023-10-01

# ─── CORS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FRONTEND_URL=http://localhost:3000
```

### Variable reference table

| Variable | File | Public? | Required | Used By |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID` | `frontend/.env.local` | Yes | Yes | Sanity client, seed scripts |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET` | `frontend/.env.local` | Yes | Yes | Sanity client |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_API_VERSION` | `frontend/.env.local` | Yes | Yes | Sanity client |
| `SANITY_API_TOKEN` | `frontend/.env.local` | No | Seeding only | Seed scripts |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL` | `frontend/.env.local` | Yes | Yes | Supabase client, middleware |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` | `frontend/.env.local` | Yes | Yes | Supabase browser client, auth |
| `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` | `frontend/.env.local` | No | Legacy only | `sync-embeddings.ts` |
| `GEMINI_API_KEY` | `frontend/.env.local` | No | Legacy only | `sync-embeddings.ts` |
| `PYTHON_BACKEND_URL` | `frontend/.env.local` | No | Yes | `/api/chat/route.ts` proxy |
| `GOOGLE_API_KEY` | `backend/.env` | No | Yes | LLM + embeddings in Python backend |
| `SANITY_PROJECT_ID` | `backend/.env` | No | Yes | Python Sanity ingestion |
| `SANITY_DATASET` | `backend/.env` | No | Yes | Python Sanity ingestion |
| `SANITY_API_TOKEN` | `backend/.env` | No | Yes | Python Sanity ingestion |
| `SANITY_API_VERSION` | `backend/.env` | No | No | Defaults to `2023-10-01` |
| `FRONTEND_URL` | `backend/.env` | No | No | FastAPI CORS; defaults to `http://localhost:3000` |

## 4. Architecture & Data Flow

### High-level system diagram

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                         Browser (User)                          |
+-------------------------------+---------------------------------+
                                | HTTP
                                v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                    Next.js 16 App Router                        |
|                                                                 |
|  +------------------+    +----------------------------------+  |
|  |  Server Components|    |  Client Components               |  |
|  |  (page.tsx files) |    |  (StateDetailClientPage, etc.)  |  |
|  |                   |    |                                  |  |
|  |  - Fetch Sanity   |    |  - Dashboard tabs & charts       |  |
|  |  - Static data    |    |  - Chat UI (streams tokens)      |  |
|  |    fallback       |    |  - Map interactions              |  |
|  +---------+---------+    +----------------------------------+  |
|            |                                                     |
|  +---------v--------------------------------------------------+ |
|  |                    API Routes (app/api/)                    | |
|  |  /api/chat  --> THIN PROXY --> Python backend               | |
|  |  /api/search --> Full-text search (Sanity GROQ)             | |
|  |  /api/subscribe --> Supabase email list                     | |
|  |  /api/digest --> Email digest trigger                       | |
|  |  /api/rht-states --> RHT state data                        | |
|  +----------------------------+-------------------------------+ |
+-------------+------------------+---------------------------------+
              |                  | HTTP proxy
              v                  v
+------------------+  +------------------------------------------+
|   Sanity CMS     |  |    Python AI Brain  (backend/main.py)    |
|                  |  |                                          |
|  - 21 schemas    |  |  FastAPI + LlamaIndex                    |
|  - GROQ queries  |  |                                          |
|  - Studio at     |  |  +------------------------------------+  |
|    /studio       |  |  |  VectorStoreIndex (LlamaIndex)      |  |
|  - Portable Text |  |  |  Persisted to backend/storage/     |  |
+------------------+  |  |                                    |  |
         ^            |  |  Sources:                          |  |
         | GROQ HTTP  |  |   - PDFs in backend/data/          |  |
         +------------+  |   - Sanity CMS (GROQ HTTP API)     |  |
                      |  +------------------+-----------------+  |
                      |                     |                     |
                      |  +------------------v-----------------+  |
                      |  |  Google Gemini Flash Lite (LLM)    |  |
                      |  |  Google text-embedding-004         |  |
                      |  +------------------------------------+  |
                      +------------------------------------------+

+------------------------------------+
|           Supabase                 |
|  - Auth (email/password)           |
|  - User sessions (middleware)      |
|  - Email subscribers table         |
+------------------------------------+
```

### AI chat flow (detailed)

```
User types question
        |
        v
POST /api/chat  (Next.js -- thin proxy only)
        |
        |  forwards entire request body + history[] unchanged
        v
POST http://localhost:8000/api/chat  (Python FastAPI)
        |
        +- 1. Reconstruct ChatMemoryBuffer from history[]
        |        |
        |        +- Re-hydrates prior user/assistant turns
        |              (sent by the frontend on every request)
        |
        +- 2. _index.as_chat_engine(chat_mode="context")
        |        |
        |        +- LlamaIndex retrieves relevant chunks
        |              from the persisted VectorStoreIndex
        |              using text-embedding-004 similarity search
        |
        +- 3. astream_chat(message)
        |        |
        |        +- Gemini Flash Lite generates response
        |              with retrieved context injected
        |
        +- 4. StreamingResponse --> token-by-token
                 |
                 +- Next.js proxy streams tokens back
                       --> ReadableStream --> browser
```

### Index build flow (startup / on-demand)

```
Backend starts  (or POST /api/ingest called)
        |
        +- Check: does backend/storage/docstore.json exist?
        |   YES --> load persisted index (~2 seconds) --> done
        |   NO  --> build from scratch:
        |
        +- 1. SimpleDirectoryReader(backend/data/)
        |       --> loads all .pdf files as LlamaIndex Documents
        |
        +- 2. fetch_sanity_content()
        |       --> GROQ HTTP API fetches 8 content types:
        |         policyAnalysis, post, academyModule, caseStudy,
        |         definition, analystNote, webinar, report
        |       --> Flattens Portable Text:
        |             string::join(body[].children[].text, " ")
        |
        +- 3. VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(all_docs)
        |       --> Embeds every document with text-embedding-004
        |       --> Builds in-memory similarity index
        |
        +- 4. index.storage_context.persist(backend/storage/)
                --> Fast startup (~2s) on all subsequent runs
```

## 5. Getting Started (Local Dev)

### Prerequisites

- **Node.js 20.x** + npm (for Next.js frontend)
- **Python 3.10+** + pip (for Python AI backend)
- Supabase project (Postgres + auth; pgvector optional — now used for auth only)
- Sanity project (free tier works)
- Google AI Studio API key (free tier: 60 req/min for Gemini, 1500 req/day for embeddings)

### Terminal A — Python AI Backend (start first)

```bash
# 1. Set up Python environment
cd backend
python3 -m venv venv          # one time only
source venv/bin/activate      # macOS/Linux
# OR: venv\Scripts\activate   # Windows

# 2. Install dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

# 3. Create backend env file
cp .env.example .env
# Fill in: GOOGLE_API_KEY, SANITY_PROJECT_ID, SANITY_DATASET, SANITY_API_TOKEN

# 4. Start the AI backend
uvicorn main:app --reload --port 8000

# First run: builds the LlamaIndex from PDFs + Sanity (~2-5 min depending on content)
# Subsequent runs: loads persisted index from backend/storage/ (~2 seconds)
# Health check: http://localhost:8000/health
```

**Adding PDFs:** Drop any `.pdf` file into `backend/data/`, then call `POST /api/ingest` to rebuild the index with the new content. No code changes needed.

### Terminal B — Next.js Frontend

```bash
# 1. Install dependencies
cd frontend
npm install

# 2. Create environment file
# Create frontend/.env.local with variables from §3
# Minimum required for local dev:
#   NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_PROJECT_ID, NEXT_PUBLIC_SANITY_DATASET
#   NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY
#   PYTHON_BACKEND_URL=http://localhost:8000

# 3. Set up Supabase (one time only)
# Open Supabase dashboard → SQL Editor → run:
# supabase/setup-rag.sql

# 4. Start development server
npm run dev
# → http://localhost:3000
# Sanity Studio: http://localhost:3000/studio (embedded, no separate process)

# 5. (Optional) Seed initial content into Sanity
npx tsx scripts/seed-content.ts
npx tsx scripts/seed-hospitals.ts
npx tsx scripts/seed-sanity-rht.ts
npx tsx scripts/seed-sanity-performance-index.ts
```

After seeding Sanity content, call `POST http://localhost:8000/api/ingest` to rebuild the AI index with the new CMS content. The Python backend automatically re-ingests Sanity on every rebuild.

### Build and lint

```bash
cd frontend
npm run build     # Production build
npm run start     # Production server
npm run lint      # ESLint
```
